items.title: The male footballers best associated with each shirt number – the readers’ edition
items.summary: Which footballers are inextricably linked to their shirt numbers? We picked out 50 players last week who have come to embody the numbers on their backs. It was not an exhaustive list – as our readers have proved. We couldn’t include some legends of the game – Pelé and Lionel Messi for a start – and
items.text:
Which footballers are inextricably linked to their shirt numbers? We picked out 50 players last week who have come to embody the numbers on their backs. It was not an exhaustive list – as our readers have proved. We couldn’t include some legends of the game – Pelé and Lionel Messi for a start – and we missed a few brilliant stories. Thankfully our readers have provided an alternative list. And, creative bunch that they are, they have begun with No 0 and ended with No 51 …
0
Hicham Zerouali
An honourable mention should go to Aberdeen’s No 0. Zerouali is one of the very few to have worn the number (before rules were changed in Scotland). He was a cult hero during a poor time at the club, who died tragically young in a car crash. Lewis
1
Bert Trautmann
The Manchester City No 1 in the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s. Your article said that Lev Yashin was an automatic choice for No 1. While mention was made of other goalkeepers, there was no nod in the direction of the great Bert Trautmann, the German prisoner of war who became a Manchester City legend. Yashin himself said “my only equal is the German boy at Manchester City”.
Bert’s goalkeeping achievements were many. He only started playing as a keeper in a prisoner of war team before signing for St Helens in the Lancashire Combination League on release from prison. A year later he signed for City, where he made more than 500 appearances as well as playing the last 17 minutes of the 1956 FA Cup final with a broken neck in the days before substitutes were allowed, making important saves towards the end to ensure a City victory. He was also the first goalkeeper voted Footballer of the Year.
Perhaps most remarkable of all, he saved 60% of penalties he faced. Unfortunately, he was not given any international recognition. As a German citizen he could not play for England and could only play for Germany if playing in the country. He would have been a certain starter in the Germany team that won the World Cup in 1954.
He also did as much as anyone to repair British-German relations after the second world war. He went from being booed by 20,000 people on his City debut to being feted by more than 50,000 fans at his 1964 testimonial. He was awarded an honorary OBE in 2004. David Cronin
3
Stuart Pearce
The greatest living Englishman; the best left-back to have played the game; the best player Nottingham Forest have ever had; and my hero (and Paolo Maldini’s). Will Kitchen
4
Billy Bremner
The captain who drove Leeds forwards for well over a decade. Captain of club and country, Bremner was the human personification of Don Revie’s team of the 1960s and 1970s. He had skill, drive, aggression, camaraderie and he played close to (and over?) the line. Thirty years after his early death, he is still the player who Leeds fans hold up as representing the qualities they value in players. It is fitting that the only player to come close to him while wearing the white No 4 was another diminutive, copper-haired Scotsman, Gordon Strachan. As the wee Scotsman with the statue outside Elland Road said: “Side before self, every time.” Nick Ramage
5
Billy Wright
Stan Cullis, the Wolves manager at the time, converted Wright from wing-half to centre-half. He was little more than 5ft 8in, which suggests he would not be a good fit in the position, but he could jump and time it right. He captained England and was the first footballer in the world to gain 100 caps. He also captained Wolves and led them to some headline victories, most notably against Honved. Most importantly of all: he represents football before 1960, when football was more open, more exciting and more rapid in the transition. Kevin R Cox
6
Bobby Moore
He was the greatest ever No 6. If Pelé described him as the best defender he ever played against, how can the Guardian not choose him? He excelled at timing, passing and the ability to read a game. He also inspired West Ham and England with his presence. Tim Evans
7
Stanley Matthews
There are still a few of us left who had the great pleasure to see the greatest No 7 of all time play, for Blackpool and Stoke City. His return to Stoke in the 1960s rejuvenated a team that had been stuck in the Second Division for a long time and helped put them back where they belonged, in the top flight. Matthews was the greatest No 7 of his day and, I would suggest, of all time. John Heath
9
Hughie Gallacher
I never saw him play but my father extolled his virtues to me. In this day and age when players are well paid, maybe overpaid, there should be a remembrance of those who went before them and created this wonderful game we call football. Nick Johnson
10
Pelé and Lionel Messi
So neither of the two greatest players to play the game, at least in my lifetime, is included. If we are talking about the beautiful game, then either Pelé (my preference) or Messi has to be the No 10. Richard Hirst
11
Mohamed Salah
Simply one of the best Premier League players this decade. His number 11 was often seen from behind, with the three defenders he was about to bamboozle looking worried in the background. Joe
15
Roberto Baggio
So obvious. Tom
16
Roy Keane
Keane was the most iconic and influential No 16. In the era of omnipresent Manchester United pundits, it’s easy to focus on the contemporary theatrical Keane playing the disgruntled, unimpressed one in the studio so well. But don’t lose sight of Keane winning duels, covering every blade of grass and spraying un-Hollywood but massively effective balls forward. Think Stadio delle Alpi, the scene where he tamed Zinedine Zidane and mounted a comeback against Juventus that enabled the Treble and all that. Think Lansdowne Road in 2001 when he essentially knocked out the Netherlands from the 2002 World Cup. Does Rodri have a movie with Steve Coogan in it? Michael Craig
18
Jürgen Klinsmann

items.title: England's All Blacks acid test, Erasmus circus, Boks to storm Dublin?
items.summary:
Nations Championship: England's All Blacks acid test at Twickenham, Rassie Erasmus circus, Springboks to storm to win vs Ireland in Dublin?
Third week of Nations Championship Tests in northern hemisphere sees England host the All Blacks in an acid test; Ireland welcome South Africa in bonkers week R
items.text:
Nations Championship: England's All Blacks acid test at Twickenham, Rassie Erasmus circus, Springboks to storm to win vs Ireland in Dublin?
Third week of Nations Championship Tests in northern hemisphere sees England host the All Blacks in an acid test; Ireland welcome South Africa in bonkers week Rassie Erasmus was handed six-Test ban; inaugural tournament concludes at Allianz Stadium Twickenham next weekend November 27-29
Thursday 19 November 2026 18:49, UK
The third weekend of Nations Championship Tests in the northern hemisphere is upon us, with England hosting the All Blacks in an acid test and Ireland facing the Springboks in the week a six-Test suspension was handed down to the controversial Rassie Erasmus...
England's All Blacks acid test
There is a sense of déjà vu, somewhat, for England this November when looking over their autumn performances and the general outlook emanating from them.
This time last year, England proved too strong for Australia and Fiji before welcoming New Zealand to Twickenham. In that Test, Steve Borthwick's side thrilled to a 33-19 victory over the All Blacks.
A nervy 27-23 win over Argentina followed, but England exited November buoyed by four wins, with many talking them up as a returning force in the world game, building towards Six Nations, Nations Championship and Rugby World Cup title tilts.
What followed was a disastrous Six Nations. The worst in England's history, in fact.
From five fixtures, they lost four for the first time ever, suffering defeat against Italy in a Test for the first time, as well as a record home loss to Ireland by a 42-21 margin at Twickenham.
They lost to Scotland for the fifth time in six years as the wheels well and truly came off a championship campaign which began with comfortable victory over a poor Wales side at home.
Displays in July's Nations Championship window were hardly overly positive either. A comprehensive 45-21 defeat in South Africa, a thrashing of a poor Fiji side in a Test bizarrely played in Liverpool, and holding on with 13 players to edge to victory in Argentina.
Borthwick and his players were suddenly under major pressure again, with stories of a camp rift emerging, but this month has seen 123 points scored in just two Tests - big victories over Australia and Japan.
Like last year, the All Blacks are coming to town with everyone wondering if England are back on track, or still a side short of the top table.
As such, Saturday's Test against a no-doubt angry New Zealand - following their shock defeat to Wales in Cardiff - represents something of an acid test for England.
Put on a show in victory, and talk of them as potentially one of the world's best will start to re-emerge. Suffer defeat, and criticism will filter back.
The circus of Rassie Erasmus
My word, it has been some week in Dublin as far as story-lines ahead of Saturday's crunch Ireland vs South Africa Test.
First, fly-half Sam Prendergast was cited for a hip-drop tackle committed against Fiji captain Peceli Yato in last week's 43-15 Ireland win - a first of its kind, with the manoeuvre outlawed at the start of this month.
Then, South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus gave the mother and father of all press conferences. Even for him - and he has quite the history - it was downright bizarre.
Off the back of the Springboks losing to France in Paris last week - clearly the reason behind Erasmus' ticking demeanour - claims and comments from South Africa's revered rugby leader ranged from extraordinary to astonishing.
He began by predicting Prendergast would get off "on a technicality" and would play in Dublin on Saturday, claiming his double Rugby World Cup-winning squad and players were treated differently at disciplinary hearings than northern hemisphere players.
Erasmus even went so far as to state "things never seem to go our way." Make of that what you will when considering he is talking about a trophy-laden side who won the last World Cup following three successive one-point knockout victories.
Far worse was to follow when Erasmus claimed "17 knee-drop tackles" by France had been missed by the referee and TMO in South Africa's defeat last week - a figure almost universally debunked when reviewed by journalists and pundits in the aftermath.
Erasmus then came out with the claims which were likely the reasoning behind World Rugby snappily handing him a six-Test suspension: questioning whether TMO's and referees were "match-fixing" and whether there was "manipulation of the game or result" of Test matches.
When a journalist at the press conference commented to Erasmus he was making a "serious intimation", his response was: "It's not an accusation."
World Rugby didn't see it that way, and though South Africa Rugby requested a formal hearing take place, Erasmus has since taken to X to confirm he will watch Saturday's Test from his Dublin hotel room and has organised a free watchalong for anyone to sign up and view him and his reaction to the Test match as it is unfolding.
The 54-year-old has now been suspended three times in five years for these sorts of incidents, which constitute "public criticism of match officials, undermining the integrity of individuals or the sport, and fuelling online abuse."
Indeed, SA Rugby have since released a statement "condemning the online abuse of officials" following confirmation of Erasmus' ban.
During the 2021 British and Irish Lions series in South Africa, after the Springboks lost the first Test, Erasmus broadcasted an hour-long critique of Australian referee Nic Berry, and was eventually handed a two-month ban from all rugby activity and 10-month matchday ban.
Berry said afterwards Erasmus' behaviour had been an "assassination of my reputation" that caused "immeasurable damage." He no longer referees Tests involving South Africa.
World Rugby found the video had contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials."
In 2022 he received a two-Test ban after sarcastic social media posts

items.text:
Dillian Whyte offers to fight Deontay Wilder on December 11: ‘If Wilder wants it, they know where I am’
Dillian Whyte has made himself available to step in for Jai Opetaia and box Deontay Wilder on the undercard of the December 11 fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff; "If they want it and they want to have a good fight, then I'm down," he said
Thursday 19 November 2026 18:07, UK
Dillian Whyte is ready to rekindle his rivalry with Deontay Wilder.
At one point Whyte was the WBC's No 1 contender when Wilder held that title. He never got to box Wilder, though did eventually challenge Tyson Fury after he'd beaten the American for the belt.
Wilder is currently looking for a new opponent after Jai Opetaia withdrew from a heavyweight bout that was scheduled for the undercard of Fury's December 11 showdown with Anthony Joshua.
Whyte has made himself available as a replacement. "If they want it then they know where I am," the Brixton heavyweight told Sky Sports News.
"If they want it and they want to have a good fight, then I'm down. You know, I always come to fight. I give it my best and I give my all.
"I've already waited 100 years for him, so if he wants it in December, then let's go."
He added: "I've been trying to fight him for 100 years. I've always believed that I could have beaten him.
"He's a big puncher, he's wiry, and he's fast and all that. I just believe that I have the mentality and the style to beat him and cause him all sorts of problems. And I still believe that."
Whyte insists he could be ready for the bill at the Principality Stadium. "I'm training to fight a week after them. So I'm in a gym, I'm looking to come back December 18. So if they want it, I'm here.
"All have to do is let me know."

items.title: US welcomes American consortium’s selection for Mrima Hill mining project
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — The United States has welcomed Kenya’s selection of a US-led consortium to develop the Mrima Hill rare earths and niobium project in Kwale County, describing the decision as a commitment to transparency and economic cooperation.
The US State Department’s Bureau of African Af
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — The United States has welcomed Kenya’s selection of a US-led consortium to develop the Mrima Hill rare earths and niobium project in Kwale County, describing the decision as a commitment to transparency and economic cooperation.
The US State Department’s Bureau of African Affairs congratulated Frontier Minerals Consortium on its selection, saying the choice of an American consortium would bring innovation, local value addition and economic opportunities to Kenya.
“Congratulations to Frontier Minerals for being selected to develop the Mrima Hill rare earths and niobium project in Kenya,” the bureau said in a statement on Thursday.
“The choice of an American consortium reflects a commitment from the Kenyan government to develop their mining sector in a transparent manner that will bring market-leading innovation to Kenya, ensure local value addition, and create jobs and economic benefits for [the United States and Kenya].”
The endorsement follows Kenya’s announcement of successful bidders for three strategic mineral projects after a competitive tender process and statutory procurement reviews.
The Ministry of Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs named Frontier Minerals Consortium as the preferred bidder for the Mrima Hill project, which targets niobium, rare earth elements and other minerals.
The consortium comprises Frontier Minerals LLC, Bunker Hill Mining Corp, ReElement Technologies and American Resources Corporation.
A joint venture between China’s Fangda Special Steel Technology Co. Ltd and Sinohydro Corporation was selected for the Kang’ura Chromite Development Project in Samburu County and the Kamacabi Copper Development Project in Tharaka Nithi County.
The government said no responsive qualifying bids were received for the Lali Hills Manganese Project in Tana River County and the Kiritiri Coltan Project in Embu County, which will be addressed separately in accordance with the law.
Licensing process still pending
The Ministry clarified that the notices issued to successful bidders were Notices of Intention to Award and did not amount to mining or prospecting licences.
The selected bidders must first engage host communities, landowners, county leadership and other relevant stakeholders, and obtain the necessary consents under the Mining Act.
They are also required to submit prospecting licence applications through the Ministry’s Online Mining Cadastre portal, accompanied by the required consents, statutory documents and fees.
The applications will then be submitted to the Mineral Rights Board for independent statutory scrutiny and recommendations before the Cabinet Secretary can grant licences.
Cabinet Secretary Hassan Ali Joho said the tender outcome should not be mistaken for immediate authorisation to begin exploration.
“An award at the end of a tender process is not a licence to immediately break ground; rather, it is the gateway to meaningful local partnership and strict regulatory compliance,” Joho said.
He said host communities should be informed about the companies seeking to operate in their areas, their technical capabilities and financial capacity, as well as their commitments to environmental protection, cultural heritage, local employment and community development.
The Ministry said the tender evaluation considered bidders’ geological and exploration expertise, plans for in-country mineral processing and beneficiation, local content, environmental restoration and financial capacity.
Successful bidders were required to attain a minimum technical score of 80 per cent before proceeding to financial evaluation.

items.title: Four arrested over brutal machete attack on Natembeya’s communication officer
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Detectives have arrested four suspects in connection with a brutal machete attack on Trans Nzoia Governor George Natembeya’s communications officer and blogger Amos Masika Boaz, popularly known as Hammer Hammer, whose vehicle was torched during a night-time ambush at his hom
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Detectives have arrested four suspects in connection with a brutal machete attack on Trans Nzoia Governor George Natembeya’s communications officer and blogger Amos Masika Boaz, popularly known as Hammer Hammer, whose vehicle was torched during a night-time ambush at his home.
The four were arrested in Kiminini Town following a coordinated manhunt by detectives from the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) Operations Support Unit and officers drawn from Trans Nzoia East, Trans Nzoia West and Kiminini.
The attack occurred on the night of November 16, 2026, at Orombe Farm in Trans Nzoia East Sub-County, shortly after Masika arrived at his compound.
According to the DCI, two masked assailants armed with machetes confronted the blogger, dragged him out of his silver Honda, registration number KDD 938D, before dousing the vehicle with petrol and setting it ablaze.
The attackers subsequently turned on him, inflicting multiple machete wounds to his head, hands and legs, leaving him seriously injured.
Masika was rushed to Reale Hospital in Kitale for emergency treatment before being referred to Eldoret for specialised medical care.
The suspects have been identified as Kennedy Nyongesa Ochieng, who detectives believe was the gang leader, Dan Wakoli Chilungu, Brian Odhiambo Odongo and Hassan Wekesa.
They remain in police custody undergoing processing ahead of their arraignment in court as investigations continue to establish the circumstances surrounding the attack and whether other individuals were involved.
The incident has sparked condemnation from Governor Natembeya, who described the assault as a calculated attempt to intimidate him and his supporters.
Speaking after the incident, Natembeya alleged that the attack was part of a broader pattern of harassment targeting his allies and county officials because of his political position.
He accused the government of orchestrating attacks against people associated with him, claims that have not been independently established.
The governor warned that violence would not force him to abandon his political stand, insisting that those behind the assault must be held accountable.
Masika’s family has also demanded answers, with his brother, Sam Masika, saying they had reported the incident to police and wanted a thorough investigation to establish who was responsible and why his brother was targeted.
The family called for those behind the attack to be brought to justice.
The arrests come amid heightened political tensions in Trans Nzoia, where Natembeya has increasingly positioned himself as a vocal critic of the national government.
However, detectives have not officially established whether the attack was politically motivated or stemmed from personal grievances.
In a statement, the DCI condemned the assault, warning that violence, intimidation and destruction of property should not be used to settle political or personal differences.
The agency said investigators were pursuing all possible leads to identify everyone involved and ensure they face the law.

items.title: Lack of Credit, Equipment Limits Women’s Gains in Agriculture
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Limited access to affordable credit and agricultural equipment is constraining the profitability of women-led agribusinesses in Kenya, despite women farmers generating higher revenue per hectare than their male counterparts.
A nine-year evaluation by the Farm to Market Allia
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 – Limited access to affordable credit and agricultural equipment is constraining the profitability of women-led agribusinesses in Kenya, despite women farmers generating higher revenue per hectare than their male counterparts.
A nine-year evaluation by the Farm to Market Alliance (FtMA) shows that women smallholders earn an average of Sh82,494 per hectare in main-season revenue, compared to Sh69,833 for men, but the productivity gains are not translating into comparable business profits.
Women-led Farmer Service Centres (FSCs) recorded average annual profits of Sh143,989, significantly lower than the Sh515,253 reported by male-led centers, exposing the financing and equipment challenges facing women entrepreneurs in the agricultural value chain.
The evaluation found that women-led centers own an average of two pieces of equipment, compared to 3.2 for male-led centers, limiting their capacity to provide mechanized services, handle larger volumes of produce and improve post-harvest management.
“The data from our nine-year journey proves beyond doubt that when women and young farmers are connected to reliable inputs, agronomic training, and structured markets, they deliver the highest returns per acre in Kenyan agriculture,” said George Njoroge, FtMA Kenya Country Coordinator.
Access to institutional financing remains another major constraint, with 70 percent of Farmer Service Centres having no formal institutional credit, despite 97 percent maintaining bank accounts.
The report attributes the financing gap partly to agricultural lending requirements that often demand land as collateral, forcing centers to rely on informal borrowing, which accounts for 20 percent of their financing.
The shortage of equipment is also contributing to post-harvest losses, particularly among women farmers.
Only 8.5 percent of Farmer Service Centres across the network own shelling or threshing equipment, with women potentially losing up to half of their bean harvest during manual drying, shelling and bagging.
Market access presents an additional challenge to the commercial growth of smallholder agriculture. Although 88.9 percent of farmers sell their produce, only 3.8 percent have formal off-taker contracts, while just 18.5 percent receive prompt payments.
The findings come as Kenya seeks to strengthen agricultural value chains and improve the commercial viability of smallholder farming, with the evaluation highlighting the need to address financing, post-harvest infrastructure and market access alongside productivity improvements.
The programme, implemented by the Cereal Growers Association since 2017, has expanded from two counties to 13, establishing 2,126 Farmer Service Centres that have reached approximately 401,955 farmers.
The centers have collectively marketed 664,009 metric tonnes of produce, while certified seed adoption among surveyed farmers has reached 88 percent.
Farmers practicing Conservation Agriculture have also recorded a 60 percent increase in main-season maize yields, rising from 2.83 metric tonnes per hectare to 4.53 metric tonnes.
However, the long-term commercial sustainability of the centers remains uncertain, with the evaluation projecting that approximately 70 percent could remain viable after programme support ends.
World Food Programme Kenya Deputy Country Director Bai Mankay Sankoh said the next phase of the programme should focus on building commercially sustainable rural enterprises rather than maintaining centers through donor funding.
“We are not trying to create a permanent network of project-supported centres. We are trying to help build viable rural enterprises that can continue serving farmers because doing so makes commercial sense,” Sankoh said.
The evaluation also identifies young people as an emerging force in agricultural enterprise, with 1,015 youth-run Farmer Service Centres employing an average of 6.1 young people each.
Youth farmers recorded average main-season maize yields of 3.6 metric tonnes per hectare, compared to 2.9 metric tonnes among older farmers, while 91 percent sold their produce into structured markets.
The report calls for targeted asset financing for women-led centers, collateral-free supply-chain credit supported by buyer contracts and improved access to digital agricultural services to address the constraints holding back rural enterprises.

items.title: Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
items.summary:
Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
For refugees, the ICJ ruling that Myanmar committed genocide is a vindication. But for many, the relief comes with a question: will they be able to return home?
Dhaka, Bangladesh — Umme Ruman was watching the news on her mobile
items.text:
Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
For refugees, the ICJ ruling that Myanmar committed genocide is a vindication. But for many, the relief comes with a question: will they be able to return home?
Dhaka, Bangladesh — Umme Ruman was watching the news on her mobile phone from her shelter in Camp 1E of the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She had been waiting for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) verdict since the afternoon. But poor internet connectivity kept interrupting the live broadcast.
Then she opened Facebook and saw a headline: “ICJ confirms Myanmar committed genocide.”
Overwhelmed, she jumped. Her sister-in-law was cooking. Ruman rushed to hug her. Before she could explain what had happened, she broke down in tears.
“I celebrated with tears of joy because, for the first time, the world acknowledged what happened to us,” she said.
On Thursday, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during brutal military operations in 2017, in which the court found more than 10,000 people had been killed.
The landmark judgement in the case, brought before the court by The Gambia, recognised the atrocities committed against the community after years of denial. For refugees who have spent nearly a decade waiting for justice, the ruling brought a wave of relief, emotion and renewed hope.
“For me, this is not simply a legal verdict. It is proof of our suffering,” Ruman said.
Across the camps, people followed the announcement on mobile phones, laptops and large screens. Some watched with friends. Others gathered with their families. Many turned to Facebook and YouTube to follow the proceedings.
Eighteen-year-old Mohammad Rehan watched with his community teacher and friends on a laptop. “Some women were crying, while others were praying to Allah,” he said. “I did not do anything special. I just sat there and listened, hoping to hear some good news that would give us a peaceful life in the future.”
For Rehan, the first thought was that the verdict could potentially open the door for the Rohingya to return home. “Just imagining that made me so happy,” he said.
The news soon spread through the blocks. Rehan said people were celebrating, while elderly refugees discussed the case and The Gambia’s role in bringing it before the court. The small West African nation was not directly affected by the violence against the Rohingya. Still, it acted as a party to the 1948 Genocide Convention, under which all member states have an obligation to prevent and address genocide. In 2022, the court ruled that The Gambia had standing to bring the case.
Rehan’s mother was also delighted when he told her about the ruling. “She was saying that we had won and that we would be able to return to our homeland,” he said.
The celebrations came against a backdrop of difficult living conditions. Rain fell over the camps on Thursday as Cyclone Akvan bore down on the Bay of Bengal, adding to the discomfort of families living in cramped shelters.
It was a reminder that while the verdict had brought recognition to their suffering, it had not changed the daily realities of refugee life. Nurul Amin, a Rohingya youth, said he was happy when the court recognised the genocide, but the announcement also brought back painful memories.
“I was happy, but I was also remembering what happened to us in 2017. I was remembering the horrific military operation, the violence I experienced and the home I had to leave behind,” he said.
Rohingya activist Rohimullah said the announcement was difficult to put into words. It reminded him of those the community had lost and the darkest days of their displacement. He described the judgement as a moment of relief and renewed hope, but said it could not bring back loved ones or erase painful memories.
Nasir Uddin, a professor of anthropology at the University of Chittagong who researches the Rohingya crisis, said the ICJ ruling was important to ensure justice and accountability from the victims’ perspective.
“In the 21st century, we talk about liberal democracy, globalisation and global justice. Yet such a massive genocide happened before our eyes. The judgement was essential to establish the concept of global justice,” he said.
Michael Kugelman, a resident senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council, said the ruling meant that Dhaka would need stronger assurances from Myanmar about the safe return of Rohingya refugees under any repatriation arrangement.
“I think that this will also have some impact on the dynamics around negotiations between Bangladesh and Myanmar on the return of Rohingya refugees, now that an international court has said that they experienced genocide,” Kugelman told Al Jazeera.
For the Rohingya, however, the hope of going home remains central. They want accountability for those responsible for the atrocities, the restoration of their rights and citizenship, and a safe and dignified return to Myanmar.
Nurul Amin said he hoped the international community would look beyond the humanitarian crisis and address the political causes of their displacement. He said he wanted freedom in Myanmar, democracy and an end to discrimination and military dictatorship.
“We are hoping this judgement will lead to something more – that we will finally be able to return home with our rights and dignity,” he said.
Maung Solaiman Shah contributed to this story.

items.title: 8 Kenyan students selected for Huawei technology training in China
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — Eight Kenyan university students are set to travel to China for specialised training in emerging technologies under Huawei’s 2026 Seeds for the Future programme.
The students were flagged off on Wednesday by the Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs ahead of their technic
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 20 — Eight Kenyan university students are set to travel to China for specialised training in emerging technologies under Huawei’s 2026 Seeds for the Future programme.
The students were flagged off on Wednesday by the Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs ahead of their technical immersion in the Chinese cities of Shenzhen and Dongguan.
Principal Secretary for Foreign Affairs Dr Abraham Korir Sing’Oei, representing Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, presided over the ceremony and handed the Kenyan flag to the delegation.
The fully funded programme will expose the students to practical training at Huawei’s research and development facilities, covering artificial intelligence (AI), 5G and 6G networks, cloud computing and digital power systems.
They will also engage in knowledge exchange with international peers as part of the initiative, which seeks to develop technical skills and nurture local ICT talent.
Sing’Oei said the programme would help bridge the gap between education, market demands and employment opportunities, while strengthening Kenya’s position in the digital economy.
“Education is the pathway for transformation, but only to the extent that we link education to markets, skills, and job creation,” he ssaid.
“By enabling students of technology and leadership in Kenya to travel to Shenzhen and interact directly with a global technology powerhouse like Huawei, we are providing a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Huawei’s investment directly strengthens Nairobi’s position as a digital leader on the African continent.”
The PS said the initiative also builds on commitments made during his official visit to Huawei headquarters in Shenzhen in August 2026.
He noted that the programme aligns with the government’s Digital Superhighway agenda under the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA), while reinforcing bilateral relations between Kenya and China.
Speaking on behalf of Huawei Technologies Kenya, Deputy Chief Executive Officer Sun Quan, also known as James, reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing local ICT talent.
“This program is named ‘Seeds for the Future.’ As these eight talented students visit Shenzhen to exchange ideas with global technical experts, our hope is that when they return, they will turn into ‘Big Trees’ that contribute significantly to Kenya’s digital economy and national development,” he said.
The ceremony was attended by government and industry representatives, including Deputy Director General for Asia Affairs Ambassador Jane B. Makori, Deputy Director for Higher Education at the State Department for Higher Education Dr Wahome Rureri, and Huawei Technologies’ Khadija Mohamed Ahmed.
Student representative Ahmed Rashid, from the University of Nairobi Faculty of Law, also delivered remarks on behalf of the selected cohort.
Launched globally in 2008, Huawei’s Seeds for the Future programme has engaged nearly 19,800 students from 143 countries and established partnerships with more than 500 universities worldwide, according to the statement.
The 2026 edition forms part of Huawei’s support for Kenya’s digital ecosystem through private-sector infrastructure, public-sector capacity building and technical skills transfer.

items.summary:
Las Vegas GP: George Russell tops practice for Mercedes as rain limits running on first day of track action
George Russell topped second practice from Pierre Gasly after there was very little running in first practice on a wet first day of track action; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with
items.text:
Las Vegas GP: George Russell tops practice for Mercedes as rain limits running on first day of track action
George Russell topped second practice from Pierre Gasly after there was very little running in first practice on a wet first day of track action; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday
Friday 20 November 2026 05:42, UK
Mercedes' George Russell topped Practice Two from Alpine's Pierre Gasly as rain limited running on the opening day of track action at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.
After no timed laps were completed in first practice due to heavy rain falling throughout, the weather relented to allow plenty of running during the second session, albeit on a damp, slowly drying circuit that prevented the use of slick tyres.
The best lap times came at the end of the session, which took place on Thursday night in Las Vegas, when Russell pipped Gasly by 0.071s, with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc three tenths off the pace in third.

- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
Leclerc and McLaren's Lando Norris, who won last time out in Brazil, had traded the fastest times for most of the session in the wetter conditions.
Norris ended up seventh, behind Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, his McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, but the times are likely to matter very little given qualifying and the race are expected to take place in dry conditions.
The schedule in Las Vegas runs a day earlier than a traditional F1 weekend, but the time difference means qualifying will take place at 4am on Saturday morning for UK viewers, with the race following at the same time on Sunday.
Remarkably, there were few incidents and the only red flag across the whole day was for a plastic bag blowing on to the circuit at the high-speed final corner in second practice.
New F1 world champion Kimi Antonelli was eighth fastest but will serve a five-place grid penalty after exceeding his internal combustion engine allocation for a second time this season.
Piastri, Williams' Carlos Sainz and Aston Martin's Lance Stroll have 10-place grid penalties for going over various power unit elements, while Haas' Oliver Bearman will start at the back.
Max Verstappen spent most of the day in the garage and completed only 10 laps in total as he finished second practice in 13th.
Verstappen, who is on a run of eight consecutive podiums, felt he had "no power" from the engine on the laps he completed and insisted "it was not normal" despite his engineer suggesting the issue was related to the power unit needing to warm up in the cold condtions.
McLaren and Mercedes have brought upgrades this weekend but the rain on Thursday meant it was virtually impossible to tell whether they made any impact.
Final practice, which gets under way at 12.30am on Saturday for UK viewers, is set to be very busy as the drivers will attempt to get plenty of dry laps in before qualifying.

items.text:
Gaza Civil Defence struggles to rescue lives as vehicles break down
More than 85 percent of Gaza Civil Defence vehicles are out of service, leaving crews struggling to reach trapped people.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Palestinian Civil Defence crews heard an explosion nearby and rushed to respond. But instead of taking a fire engine – the only vehicle available to the team at the time – they had to grab their equipment and rush to help on foot. The fire engine wasn’t working.
“We heard the strike, opened the vehicle, took our equipment and ran,” said Abdullah al-Majdalawi, a Civil Defence field officer, describing the response to an Israeli attack near the al-Qattan Centre on November 3. It took about 10 minutes for the crew to reach the site, carrying their equipment, and then carrying injured people back. They also recovered the body of someone killed in the strike.
It was another example of how the breakdown of emergency vehicles is affecting rescue teams’ ability to reach people quickly.
In a separate incident in southern Gaza City’s Sabra neighbourhood last month, the vehicle the Civil Defence team was using broke down while the crew was responding to an Israeli air strike on the area.
By the time they were able to reach the scene, several people had been killed, and others were critically injured. Al-Majdalawi believes that arriving sooner could have given some of the injured a better chance of survival.
During another mission, in 2024, the crew had to rely on a man with a donkey-drawn cart to transport them and their equipment.
“People were astonished to see Civil Defence personnel travelling that way… but this is what we can do,” al-Majdalawi said.
An ageing fleet, dwindling capacity
The only dedicated rescue vehicle in Gaza governorate, a Toyota Hilux pick-up truck, has been out of service for weeks. It is more than 20 years old, according to al-Majdalawi, and has been worn down by years of use and the intense workload during Israel’s genocidal war, which began in October 2023.
The crew has tried everything to keep it running, including patching its tyres with flour dough when proper repairs were not possible. The vehicle needs a power steering pump, tyres and other parts. Its turbo system is also faulty, while problems with its lights make night-time missions more dangerous.
“We have exhausted every means and every method to keep this vehicle running,” al-Majdalawi said.
Without it, crews have to rely on larger fire engines for rescue operations. These are harder to manoeuvre through streets crowded with tents, makeshift shelters, and market stalls.
If emergencies happen simultaneously in different areas, and there aren’t enough vehicles available, teams have to choose where to respond first.
The situation reflects a wider collapse in the capacity of Gaza’s Civil Defence.
Emergency teams are still responding to strikes, fires, and building collapses, but their ability to reach people is increasingly constrained by a lack of functioning vehicles and equipment.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned in a May 1 report that restrictions on the entry of engine oil and spare parts for vehicles and rubble-removal machinery were having an increasingly severe impact on humanitarian operations in Gaza.
It said prolonged shortages were causing vehicles and generators to break down beyond repair, affecting the movement of humanitarian teams, ambulance services, and other essential operations.
Raed al-Dahshan, director of Gaza City’s Civil Defence, said more than 85 percent of the department’s vehicles were out of operation, leaving only about 15 percent working across the territory.
Many vehicles have been in service since 1994, when the Palestinian Authority was established, and have carried out tens of thousands of missions. Years of use, damaged roads, and the demands of the war have left much of the fleet worn out.
Al-Dahshan said many Civil Defence vehicles have exceeded their expected service life and urgently need replacing. International fire-service guidelines generally recommend replacing front-line fire engines after 15 to 20 years of operation.
Repairs without the parts
Repairing the vehicles has become increasingly difficult. Local workshops have limited capacity, and the department often has to refurbish old parts or find alternatives because replacement parts are unavailable.
At the department’s maintenance workshop, maintenance officer Abd al-Fattah al-Nimra works alongside a team trying to keep the ageing fleet operational.
With proper parts unavailable or prohibitively expensive, mechanics resort to temporary fixes and substitute components. These may get a vehicle moving again, but they cannot offer the reliability or performance of the original parts.
“Since the beginning of the war, we have faced many problems with spare parts and their high prices,” al-Nimra said. “The parts that run out are not replaced because the occupation prevents them from entering.”
He said the team tried to find temporary alternatives wherever possible, but they did not perform as well as original components. Even basic items such as tyres had become extremely expensive, while the cost and shortage of engine oil added another burden to already limited maintenance budgets.
Since the beginning of the war in October 2023, Israeli restrictions on the entry of essential supplies into Gaza, including vehicle spare parts and engine oil, have made it increasingly difficult for emergency services to maintain their fleets.
OCHA warned that shortages of these supplies were causing vehicles and generators to break down, in some cases beyond repair, while also affecting heavy machinery needed to remove rubble and keep essential services running.
The only rescue vehicle serving Gaza governorate needs a power steering pump, tyres, a turbo component and warning lights identifying it as a rescue vehicle, al-Nimra said. Although some parts can be found in the local mark

items.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers
items.summary: The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the perma
items.text:
The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.
Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.
Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.
The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.
One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”
The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.
Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.
A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.
Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.
In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.
Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.
Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.
But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.
It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.
Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.
The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.
In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.
In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.
Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be cons

items.text:
Contaminated petrol leaves Yemeni drivers struggling to make ends meet
Drivers in Houthi-controlled areas face rising fuel prices and costly repairs as contaminated petrol damages their cars.
Sanaa, Yemen – Yazan, 28, filled up his car at a petrol station in Sanaa and began a trip towards the city of Ibb to the south.
The journey would usually take about two and a half hours, but as he accelerated along the road, Yazan noticed that the car was struggling to pick up speed.
Yazan, who did not want to give his full name, explained that the harder he pressed the accelerator, the more the engine vibrated. The unusual engine noise and vibration forced him to stop several times on the road.
It eventually took Yazan six hours to reach his destination. He believes the problem was caused by contaminated petrol – fuel mixed with oil and impurities – that he bought in Sanaa.
“The petrol left numerous cars, including mine, with many faults,” Yazan told Al Jazeera. “We pay for the expensive petrol that damages our engines.”
Yazan is not alone. Other drivers in Sanaa have reported similar problems with contaminated and increasingly expensive petrol.
The cause of the issue is disputed. In June, the Sanaa-based Yemen Petroleum Company (YPC), run by the Houthis who have controlled northwest Yemen since 2014, said contaminated fuel was the result of inadequately equipped fuel storage facilities in Hodeidah.
Fuel storage tanks in the port city and the nearby Ras Isa oil terminal have been attacked by Israeli and United States air strikes since 2024, in response to Houthi attacks on Israel and shipping in the Red Sea.
The YPC said that the tanks allowed the company to remove impurities before pumping fuel to the market. With the facilities not functioning, the quality of the fuel is impacted.
But many Yemenis dispute that explanation. According to the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, restrictions on fuel imports have led the Houthis to partly rely on importing lower-quality Iranian fuel.
Mohammed Ansi, a Yemeni academic, said regular people were being exploited.
“Fuel shipments are being brought in without any accountability, oversight, or conscience – driven solely by the desire for profit and commissions,” he said.
Fuel imports fell sharply from January to May this year. Compared to the same period in 2025, they fell 73 percent through Houthi-controlled ports and 60 percent through ports controlled by the Yemeni government, according to the World Bank.
The drop is partly a result of the impact of the US-Israeli war on Iran on oil shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as damage to Yemen’s ports from the various attacks it has faced.
Costly repairs
With the crisis continuing, its financial toll on families is mounting amid the escalating war in Yemen.
“Paying for expensive petrol and vehicle repair is a fresh war on our livelihoods. It is draining us,” said Yazan.
A few weeks ago, 20 litres (5.3 gallons) of petrol cost 9,500 Yemeni riyals ($18 at rates set by the Houthis) in Sanaa. The price has since risen to 11,400 Yemeni riyals ($21), an increase of 20 percent.
That is not taking into account the additional repair costs necessary if contaminated fuel gets into a vehicle’s engine.
Yemenis are already struggling to make ends meet, a situation that has gotten worse over a decade of war.
An April report by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said that Yemen’s conflict has led to significant macroeconomic vulnerabilities and a marked decrease in income per capita, leaving more than half of the population in urgent need of humanitarian assistance.
Akram Naji, a taxi driver in Sanaa, is among those struggling to get by, and he is now having to figure out how to pay to fix his car.
Naji said he visited a mechanic in Sanaa’s Maeen district after he heard a strange noise coming from his vehicle’s engine.
“The mechanic identified mechanical problems, including a faulty fuel pump, clogged fuel injectors and reduced engine performance.”
Repairing the damage cost him 55,000 Yemeni riyals (about $100), he said.
“For many taxi drivers here like myself, paying this amount of money immediately is a challenge,” Naji said. “I had to not pay my rent in full and decreased my family’s daily expenses to cover the maintenance costs.”
Ali Beidhani, a mechanical engineer in Sanaa, explained what happens when the contaminated petrol enters a vehicle.
“As I observed, when this oily substance or impurities enter the engine along with the petrol, they accumulate in the combustion system,” Beidhani said. “As this substance is exposed to high temperatures, it becomes highly viscous, almost like glue. This leads to damage to engine valves, clogged fuel injectors, and engine vibrations.”
In severe cases, it can even lead to complete engine failure, Beidhani noted.
He said he had seen many drivers struggle to afford repairs.
“The repair cost could force drivers to borrow money or sell possessions like gold, especially if the engine gets damaged or completely fails. Those who rely on their vehicles to eke out a living suffer the most,” said Beidhani.
Deepening humanitarian crisis
Wafiq Saleh, an economic researcher and executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni-Gulf Studies, told Al Jazeera that the spread of contaminated fuel heightens the misery of civilians in the war-torn country.
“Bus or taxi driver or delivery riders or farmers struggle every day to make ends meet. With the spread of contaminated petrol, their jobs are disrupted, and they may find themselves incapable of feeding their families,” said Saleh.
He argues that the authorities in Sanaa “bear full responsibility for importing substandard fuel or supplying the market with adulterated petrol, taking advantage of the lack of accountability”.
“The proliferation of adulterated fuel drains citizens’ savings and threatens the livelihoods of thousands of drivers. Breadwinners shift their focus from feeding their children to fixing their vehicle engines,”

items.text:
UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
- Published
Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.
The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.
The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.
A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.
The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.
In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.
Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.
Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.
The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.
Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.
"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.
"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.
"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."
Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.
The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.
- The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs? 
  - Published3 days ago
- The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left 
  - Published2 days ago
An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.
The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.
However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.
Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.
Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.
Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.
However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.
He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".
She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough".
"We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

items.text:
White House replaces cyber security chief after tech outages
November 20, 2026
Sean Cairncross is exiting his post as White House national cyber director after a series of technology-related outages in the United States over the week led to disruptions in air travel, banking and national security networks.
Shortly after Axios and other US news outlets first reported Cairncross' departure on Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the Pentagon's Chief Information Officer, Kirsten Davies, as the new cyber director, congratulating her on X.
"Look forward to working together to strengthen America's cybersecurity," Rubio said.
Davies will assume the position in an acting capacity, media outlets reported citing White House officials.
"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," Davies wrote on X late Thursday night, as she thanked US President Donald Trump and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller for their "faith and steady confidence" in her.
"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth referred to Davies' tenure at the Pentagon as one in which "she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional."
"We are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape," the Pentagon chief said.
Cairncross leaves after US tech outages
The Trump administration came under scrutiny in recent days after the US witnessed a major tech meltdown as service outages affected not just travel, communications, and e-commerce, but also the National Security Agency.
Top US officials have since sought to assure people in the country that there was no evidence of a cyberattack.
In 2025, Trump nominated Cairncross to serve as his top adviser on cybersecurity and data protection policy. He was subsequently confirmed to the post by the Senate.
During Trump's first stint in the Oval Office, Cairncross took on various roles as a White House insider. He was also an executive at the Republican National Committee before becoming the cybersecurity chief.

items.text:
CINCINNATI -- On a night of mixed emotions, Mauricio Pochettino tried to make the moment last as long as possible.
After the final whistle blew, confirming the United States men's national team's 2-0 win over Haiti in the quarterfinals of the Concacaf Nations League, Pochettino was officially no longer the manager of the USMNT. He is now the manager of Manchester United. But he still wanted to savor the moment. He gave hugs to just about everyone in sight: players, coaches, even U.S. Soccer executives JT Batson and Oguchi Onyewu. He took a photo with the entire USMNT staff.
Pochettino completed his requisite postgame news conference, where he said the U.S. players will "achieve big things" in the future. But there was one last team talk to give. That took place in the locker room. There was happiness at the victory. Sadness that Pochettino would no longer take part in the USMNT's journey.
"That was flood works for many people, but it's bound to happen," said U.S. forward Folarin Balogun, referring to the tears that were shed. "We had a really close relationship between his staff and us as players. I think he was really connected."
U.S. captain Tyler Adams said Pochettino had to "calm himself when it got too emotional."
As send-offs go, Tuesday's win over Haiti was about as good as could be expected for Pochettino's last game in charge. Given that the U.S. carried a six-goal cushion into the match from the first leg, it was a game for managing the result as well as the emotions. Sure, the U.S. wasn't quite as clinical in front of goal in this match as it was in the first leg, but the goals the team did score were of high quality. Christian Pulisic scored on a bicycle kick from Weston McKennie's cross in the 25th minute, and Julian Hall doubled the lead just before halftime, deftly taking McKennie's lofted pass and then lifting his shot just over Alexandre Pierre in the Haiti goal. The result made for an 8-0 victory for the U.S. on aggregate.
At which point the long goodbye that had lasted for the past 10 days accelerated. Pochettino's nickname during his playing days was "The Sheriff," given the way he commanded his team's back line as a central defender. On Tuesday, his role of sheriff was more cinematic in nature, making like one of those lawmen in a Hollywood Western. In his view, his work was done. It was time to move on to the next stop to revive a team's fortunes, in this case Manchester United.
It's an exit like no other manager in U.S. men's national team history has experienced. None of his full-time predecessors, at least in the modern era, left of their own accord. Some, such as Bora Milutinovic and Bruce Arena (version 1.0), were nudged aside. Others, such as Steve Sampson, Jurgen Klinsmann and Arena (version 2.0), were shoved out the door.
Not so for Pochettino. Hence the mixed emotions. The Argentine was largely given a hero's send-off Tuesday. After the match, fans chanted "Poch-e-tti-no." "Take Me Home, Country Roads" blared over the loudspeakers one last time. Pochettino soaked in the adulation, applauding the fans. Yet all of this was happening in spite of the fact that he's leaving less than three months after signing a new contract with U.S. Soccer. At the least, there has been an acknowledgment that departing for a higher-profile job is how things work at the highest levels of the sport. There are only so many coaching jobs at the same level as Manchester United. It still makes for an odd dynamic, though it's one the players accept.
"That's football, and that's the world of football," said midfielder Weston McKennie about Pochettino's departure prior to Tuesday's match. "You say goodbyes, and new people come in, and you get used to it after playing a long time in this type of level."
Some emotions have more clarity. Pochettino has projected a vibe these past 10 days of a man torn in two, conflicted between a job with U.S. Soccer that he enjoyed, and that of Manchester United, one he has wanted for much of his managerial career. The reality isn't as muddled. Certainly, Pochettino is appreciative of how he was treated by U.S. Soccer throughout his USMNT tenure, especially after his experience at Chelsea fell short of his expectations. He was treated with honesty and respect, and more critically, allowed to get on with the work of constructing a team for the FIFA World Cup. He also created a genuine bond with the players. That was very real.
But make no mistake, Pochettino didn't have to think twice about taking the Manchester United job. Being sensitive to the feelings of his bosses at U.S. Soccer, and having fond memories of being in charge of the USMNT -- and even shedding a tear or two -- is not the same thing as having to make an agonizing decision. The negotiations were done and dusted inside of a week. Following Saturday's 6-0 blowout of Haiti in the first leg, half of Pochettino's staff, including top assistant Jesus Perez, departed for Manchester to get on with the business of starting their new adventure.
The lack of internal conflict was also made clear during a roundtable with reporters on Monday. This is a man very much looking forward to the future with excitement. There will be no looking back.
"It's true that when I arrive at this type of possibility, like United, you say, 'Yes, I want that,'" he said. "I want to prove again myself."
Yet the mixed emotions were there until the very end. The last person Pochettino hugged postmatch was none other than Pulisic. The two have certainly endured some ups and downs in their relationship during Pochettino's tenure with the USMNT. Viewed from the outside, there was professionalism, but little warmth. Perhaps that began to thaw a little at the very end. The team-first ethos of Pochettino had imprinted itself on Pulisic.
"We're happy that we could obviously send [Pochettino] off in a good manner like that," Pulisic said. "[Winning] feels good like it always does. I think I still want to be part of this team and it wa

items.title: Which USMNT fringe players stand to benefit from Mauricio Pochettino's exit?
items.summary:
At the risk of stating the obvious, it's tough to earn a call-up for a national team.

items.text:
At the risk of stating the obvious, it's tough to earn a call-up for a national team.
For the United States men, who have seen a rise in players moving to more competitive leagues in Europe, this is no different. Long gone are the days in which simply playing in the Premier League or representing a UEFA Champions League-level club is enough to guarantee a national team spot.
More depth and talented options are clearly a positive for the U.S, but that also means that the number of high-profile players who may not get an opportunity on the international stage has also increased. Whether it be due to a player's skill or simply not fitting into a manager's vision, there are a handful of established players who found minutes under Mauricio Pochettino hard to come by.
But with Pochettino now on the ground at Manchester United, the outlook for the national team squad has been reset. With a yet-to-be-named replacement on the horizon, who are the players who could benefit the most in a new era for the USMNT?
Aidan Morris | 25 | Midfielder | Middlesbrough
Games: 7 (tied for 32nd most in Pochettino era)
Consistent minutes for an English Championship side that nearly got promoted to the Premier League? Check. Previous domestic success as an MLS All-Star and two-time MLS Cup champion? Check. Praise in Europe from well-respected coaches? Check.
A key role for the USMNT? Apparently not.
This perhaps says more about a crowded pool of midfielders for the U.S., but Morris claimed just one appearance for Pochettino this year during a March friendly against Portugal. Since then, he's been on the outside looking in, but if he continues to show off his traits as a well-rounded central midfielder, the next coach may be willing to give him more opportunities.
Still just 25, he could be at the peak of his abilities by the time the 2028 Copa América and 2030 FIFA World Cup roll around.
Yunus Musah | 23 | Midfielder | AC Milan
Games: 9 (T-28th most in Pochettino era)
Musah's 2026 World Cup fate appeared cemented as soon as he decided to take a break from the 2025 Gold Cup, due to fatigue. Coupled with sporadic minutes in Serie A on loan with Atalanta, Musah was not only absent from the World Cup roster, but went more than 18 months without a national team call-up between March 2025 and September 2026.
The good news is that he's still just 23 years old, and in a more prominent role under Ruben Amorim that has provided much-needed minutes, the versatile midfielder has once again showcased that he can play in a handful of different positions.
And don't forget: Even though he missed out on 2026's edition, Musah was one of the USMNT's breakout stars of the 2022 World Cup.
Joe Scally | 23 | Defender | Borussia Mönchengladbach
Games: 13 (T-19th most in Pochettino era)
To be fair, of the five players on this list, Scally did go to the 2026 World Cup. In fact, the fullback earned a start in one group stage game.
Nonetheless, for an American who is a consistent starter in the Bundlesliga, it's probably a letdown to be typically third choice in the right-back depth chart. Alex Freeman is the clear favorite as the starter in that spot, but could the next coach begin to favor backup minutes for a more defensive-minded and adaptable defender like Scally?
He's been linked to bigger clubs in the past, and if he moves to a more noteworthy side, that could make things interesting in the fight for minutes across the back line.
Johnny Cardoso | 25 | Midfielder | Atlético Madrid
Games: 6 (T-35th in Pochettino era)
On paper, Cardoso should be a USMNT star. He's well-versed in the Champions League and plays for a genuine powerhouse in global soccer that is Atlético Madrid.
There are two problems, though. One, he has missed 19 games through injury since making the move to the Spanish capital in July 2025, making it hard for him to demonstrate any form or fitness at club level -- including suffering a May ankle injury that ruled him out of the World Cup. And two, when he has been fit enough to feature for the national team, he's been prone to costly errors that are completely antithetical to what he has shown in LaLiga.
Now fit after resuming play in August, it's only a matter of time before the next USMNT coach attempts their own roll of the dice when it comes to finding a place for the defensive midfielder.
Tanner Tessmann | 25 | Midfielder | Lyon
Games: 12 (T-22nd most in Pochettino era)
There are some similarities between Tessmann and Cardoso. Both, on paper, had the résumé to shine with the USMNT, but looked more like a square peg in a round hole.
Twelve appearances are still a decent number, but his omission from Pochettino's World Cup roster was a surprise. Although he had suffered a muscle injury before the tournament, the expectation was that he would be fit by the start of the World Cup.
Aggressive, but also possessing the ability to provide accurate distribution and the occasional shot from distance, Tessmann could be back in the mix soon.
