Thousands of Colombians have taken to the streets in a second nationwide protest against President Abelardo de la Espriella, op
items.text:
Thousands protest Colombia’s tax plans amid row over US military role
Trade unions, students and opposition groups demonstrated in Bogota and other major cities on Thursday
Thousands of Colombians have taken to the streets in a second nationwide protest against President Abelardo de la Espriella, opposing proposed tax reforms and rising living costs as his government faces scrutiny over plans for closer military cooperation with the United States.
Trade unions, students and opposition groups demonstrated in Bogota and other major cities on Thursday against proposals to lower the income tax threshold, increase healthcare contributions and reduce corporate taxes.
“A large part of Colombia feels vulnerable. The rich are the ones who are getting more money,” Leidy Gutierrez, a 21-year-old psychology student, told the AFP news agency.
The proposed reforms would require Colombians earning more than about $985 a month to pay income tax, down from the current threshold of about $1,419.
De la Espriella’s government says the measures are necessary to raise revenue amid a fiscal crisis, with next year’s deficit projected to reach 9.4 percent of gross domestic product. The president has already withdrawn a controversial proposal to raise taxes on basic food products following widespread criticism.
Former President Gustavo Petro, who has backed the demonstrations, urged Colombians to mobilise against policies he said threatened household incomes.
De la Espriella said citizens were free to demonstrate peacefully but warned that he would not tolerate road blockades or what he described as “urban terrorism”.
The marches were mostly peaceful, but some ended in clashes with riot police, who fired tear gas and water cannon, AFP reported.
Row over US military operations
The demonstrations came as the president and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth rejected a New York Times report claiming Bogota had turned down a proposal for joint US-Colombian military operations against drug trafficking groups on Colombian territory.
The newspaper reported on Wednesday, citing US officials, that de la Espriella had told Washington he lacked sufficient support in Congress to authorise the operations, prompting Hegseth to shorten his visit to Colombia.
A US official told the Reuters news agency that concerns existed in Bogota over congressional support but did not confirm that the Colombian president had rejected the proposal outright.
De la Espriella denied rejecting any proposal from US President Donald Trump’s administration, saying cooperation with Washington was aimed at strengthening Colombia’s military capabilities rather than seeking the deployment of American troops. He stressed that any such deployment would require congressional approval.
During his visit to Bogota on Wednesday, Hegseth praised Colombia’s participation in the US-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, an initiative aimed at strengthening regional military cooperation against organised crime.
The protests were the second nationwide mobilisation since de la Espriella took office in August. Tens of thousands demonstrated in October against what opposition groups described as an erosion of human rights and social reforms introduced under Petro.

items.text:
Lula visits ailing Chief Raoni as Brazil recognises Indigenous land
Brazil declared Kapot Nhinore the permanent land of the Mebengokre and Yudja peoples, a step towards formal demarcation.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has visited the ailing Indigenous leader Raoni Metuktire, a lifelong defender of the Amazon rainforest, as the country’s government recognised the chief’s ancestral land as Indigenous territory.
Lula met the 94-year-old chief on Thursday in Peixoto de Azevedo, a city in Mato Grosso state, near the Amazonian village where Raoni has lived for decades.
Raoni, who is known for his wooden lip plate, is receiving palliative care for gastrointestinal cancer and was hospitalised for a few days last week with a lung infection and low blood pressure.
“There is no Brazilian more authentic than our comrade Raoni,” Lula said. “He represents the past, he represents the present, and his ideas represent the future of Indigenous peoples in this country.”
At a ceremony later, Brazil’s Justice Ministry declared the Kapot Nhinore Indigenous Territory to be in the permanent possession of the Mebengokre, also known as Kayapo, and Yudja peoples. It is a crucial step towards formal demarcation of the land by presidential decree. Raoni has campaigned for its protection for three decades.
Lula said he was “deeply distressed” to hear of Raoni’s hospitalisation while he was at the COP31 climate summit in Turkiye. “I wanted to resolve the issue regarding the land where Raoni was born while he was still alive,” he said.
Raoni’s grandson, Roiti Metuktire, told the AFP news agency the decision had come as a surprise to the family. “It’s his last wish,” he said.
Why it matters
Raoni left his home in the Amazon in the late 1980s to travel the world, meeting presidents, popes and royals to warn about the destruction of the planet’s biggest rainforest. He walked beside Lula at his inauguration in 2023.
Experts see demarcated Indigenous territories as one of the best barriers against deforestation, as the Amazon moves closer to a tipping point at which it could become a drier, savannah-like ecosystem.
The territory covers about 362,000 hectares (nearly 900,000 acres). Eloy Terena, Brazil’s minister of Indigenous peoples, said it is 84 percent forest.
A 2023 Greenpeace report said more than 47,000 hectares (116,000 acres) were used for pasture or soy.
A battle ahead
Rural producers have campaigned against the demarcation, saying it would have severe economic consequences for thousands of non-Indigenous people who live and farm there.
“There is still a bit of a battle ahead. There are over two hundred properties on this land,” Lula said.
Brazil has almost 800 Indigenous lands, about 60 percent of them fully regularised. Lula resumed demarcations after returning to office in 2023, with 20 territories fully demarcated in three years. They remain under pressure from agribusiness, illegal gold mining and logging.
This week, about 20 emaciated members of an isolated Indigenous group emerged from the forest in another part of the Amazon to ask for food, highlighting the challenges faced by Indigenous communities nationwide.

items.text:
Asia’s stock markets dive as Anthropic debut fails to allay AI bubble fears
Indexes in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong fall amid tech sell-off.
Asian stock markets have opened to steep losses as fears that the AI boom is unsustainable continue to weigh on sentiment despite Anthropic’s blockbuster debut.
Markets in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong fell sharply on Friday, as investor excitement around the AI giant’s public listing failed to ally concerns about the sustainability of the multi-trillion-dollar investments propping up the sector.
Tokyo’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and Seoul’s Kospi each tumbled about 4.5 percent in morning trading, while the Taiex in Taipei plunged nearly 6 percent.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index dipped as much as 2 percent.
The sell-off reflects concerns that AI-led growth is slowing down and the “peak growth phase” may have passed, said Rajat Agarwal, an Asia equity strategist with Societe Generale.
“The second element is on the demand vacuum that we are seeing,” Agarwal told Al Jazeera.
“At the time when foreigners are not buying, it is to be seen how long can the domestic investors stay put, particularly in Korea, on which the drawdown has been more severe.”
Like Wall Street, Asia’s main bourses are heavily exposed to AI.
The region is home to some of the key players in the global AI ecosystem, including South Korean memory chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, Taiwanese contract chipmaker TSMC, and Japanese investment holding company Softbank Group.
Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI in recent year, stoking fears of a speculative market bubble similar to the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.
Global AI-related investment is projected to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.
Market sentiment has been further dampened by moves in Washington to clampdown on China’s access to advanced chips amid claims that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a Chinese intelligence operative or asset.
The US Bureau of Industry and Security this week announced new export licence requirements aimed at preventing Chinese AI developers from remotely accessing top-of-the-line compute power at data centres in third countries, mainly in Southeast Asia,
The market retreat in Asia followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, even as Anthropic shares jumped 17 percent on their first day of trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York.
Anthrophic’s stock price rose as high as $111 before settling just about $97, vaulting the Claude creator into the ranks of the world’s most valuable companies.
The San Francisco-based AI giant’s market debut came after it raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, leapfrogging the previous record of $75bn set by SpaceX in June.
Despite the excitement around Anthrophic, key indexes closed in the red, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropping 2.3 percent and the broader S&P500 falling 2 percent.

items.text:
EU and UK set to sign deals on trade, energy, youth mobility at Brussels summit
The UK and the EU are poised to agree new deals on trade, energy and youth mobility at a summit in Brussels on Friday, as part of UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's bid to reset ties with the bloc. Burnham – who has said he hopes to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime – argues the deals will help fix some of the damage Brexit inflicted.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the EU's top officials hope to seal deals to ease trade and youth mobility at a Brussels summit Friday, billed as a first step in his push to rebuild ties after Brexit.
Since taking power this summer, Burnham has smashed through the taboos in Britain's toxic debate over relations with Europe – going as far as to float rejoining the bloc one day.
For now the summit with EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa will focus on much smaller steps to help turn the page a decade after the UK voted to leave – while Burnham saves for later the bigger decisions on what could come next.
"It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive – to deliver a win-win for Britain and the EU," Burnham said this week.
"After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship."
Read moreBurnham sets out 'new path' for Britain, vows to seek consensus on ties with EU
On the table in Brussels are three main agreements: a deal cutting red tape for food exports, another linking the two sides' emissions-trading schemes and a third on a "youth experience scheme".
Burnham argues those moves – which were in the pipeline long before he entered Downing Street – will help fix some of the damage Brexit inflicted.
British firms will export to Europe more easily again and thousands of under-30s will be allowed to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel.
But while the mood music at the meeting with EU chiefs von der Leyen and Costa may be much improved, old habits still die hard.
Brussels and London wrangled ferociously down to the wire over the details, with EU states greenlighting the deal package late Thursday night according to multiple diplomats, but a final sign-off still needed from the UK side.
One key sticking point was on pinning London down to a future agreement on cutting fees for EU students at UK universities to the level paid by their British counterparts.
Maros Sefcovic, the EU's veteran pointman on UK talks, insisted the atmosphere had stayed "very positive" – "even if the negotiations are very detailed and sometimes very, very hard".
'Tread carefully'
Burnham pledged not to "re-run" the Brexit debate if he became prime minister but has risked doing just that since succeeding Keir Starmer in July.
Having previously said he'd like to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime, the former Manchester mayor has promised to lay out options that could range from leaving things as they are to entering the customs union or becoming a member again.
The strategy is in part because polls now regularly indicate most Britons regret Brexit and would vote to re-enter the bloc if a referendum was held tomorrow.
It is also reflective of Britain's weak economy, damaged by Brexit, and how much the world has changed since 2016, with Europe firmly behind Ukraine in its war against Russian aggression.
Burnham hopes friendlier EU relations will help build a broad centre-left coalition to win the next general election, not anticipated until 2029.
But the strategy comes with huge risks, not least because his own party – never mind the country – is divided on how to proceed.
For now, the prime minister appears to have tempered his early urgency.
"I'm happy with closer ties but he does need to tread carefully," one Labour MP told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Burnham's push leaves him open to accusations of Brexit betrayal from the opposition Conservatives and hard-right Reform UK party of Nigel Farage – who will give his own press conference in Brussels Friday.
The prime minister has committed to Starmer's "red lines" on Europe for this parliament, meaning no return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.
But calls to go further are getting louder – with former deputy prime minister David Lammy becoming the highest-profile Labour figure to urge putting rejoining the EU in the party's next election manifesto.
In Brussels meanwhile, there is little expectation the UK will return to the fold any time soon.
"I doubt he'd take the risk of a major step that would be so radioactive," said one senior EU diplomat.
"He'll probably keep on trying to nibble away around the edges to improve ties -- and we are open to have as close a relationship as possible."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.summary:

The brilliant young winger had his shot deflected for an own goal on the hour and th
items.text:
Sydney FC prodigy Akol Akon has demonstrated why he’s one of the most exciting talents in Australian football, leading the Joeys to a shock 2-0 victory over Argentina to launch their U17 World Cup campaign in style.
The brilliant young winger had his shot deflected for an own goal on the hour and then produced an audaciously cheeky finish 11 minutes later to seal the opening-day win on Friday (AEDT) as Carl Veart’s side announced their return to the global boys’ competition for the first time in seven years.
Against one of the powerhouse football nations, Australia had their backs to the wall, having to make 31 clearances as Argentina enjoyed two-thirds of the possession and 22 shots on goal. But the Joeys fought back after the break, spearheaded by Akon, who hailed their second-half heist as “amazing”.
The 17-year-old livewire provided the real star quality, and it was soon evident why the Sky Blues had wanted to keep him in Australia for their A-League Men campaign instead of releasing him for the tournament; a decision that triggered widespread backlash before being reversed.
Akon caused havoc from the start down the right flank, his neat through ball in the fifth minute almost resulting in a goal for Central Coast Mariners’ Luke Becvinovski.
The teenage sensation then struck after the break following another dangerous foray down the right that ended with his shot across goal deflecting off the hapless Alvaro Guich and into the net.
In the 71st minute, Mariners midfielder Oli O’Carroll expertly picked off an Argentina attack before Brisbane’s Emmett Shaw released Akon with a slide-rule left-foot pass, the winger going on to dummy the goalkeeper before slotting into an empty net.
It only got worse for Argentina when substitute Benjamin Vallejos got sent off for a reckless challenge in stoppage time.
But it wasn’t all about Akon, a considerable talent who’s already made his national U23 bow. At the other end, Charlie Wilson-Papps, the young goalkeeper who’s on the books at Brighton and Hove Albion, made half-a-dozen fine saves and kept a clean sheet.
“I do it for my teammates, I do it for my family at home, so to make them proud is is the most important thing,” said Akon as he clutched the player-of-the-match trophy afterwards.
Akon’s only worry came with the video checking of his goal. “Ah, that was nerve-racking, man,” he said. “Because at 1-0, it was a very scary game. So to be able to seal it like that, the coach was telling me it was a goal.
“The first goal? It wasn’t really my goal, but I just wanted to do the Tim Cahill, start off the tournament like that. So, yeah, the knee side had to come with it.
“Now, the group, we’re really confident, really confident in our ability, and I think that showed today.”
Next up on Sunday for the Joeys will be Denmark, who lost 4-0 to Mozambique in their Group C opener on Thursday.

items.summary:
Meta rethinks 2030 climate goals as AI data centres drive emissions up
Rising data center energy needs force Meta to adjust its sustainability targets amid growing corporate climate retreat.
Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, has said it is reconsidering its 2030 deadline for reaching net-ze
items.text:
Meta rethinks 2030 climate goals as AI data centres drive emissions up
Rising data center energy needs force Meta to adjust its sustainability targets amid growing corporate climate retreat.
Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, has said it is reconsidering its 2030 deadline for reaching net-zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, in the latest sign of a broad corporate retreat from climate pledges.
The company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing and interim milestones, including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal”, Rachel Peterson, Meta’s vice president of data centres, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, said in the company’s annual sustainability report on Thursday.
Meta reported that its net carbon-equivalent emissions rose 45 percent in 2025 to 11.8 million tonnes, a figure that is itself based on accounting methods that climate advocates view with scepticism.
“When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned. The reality has been far more complex,” the executives wrote in the report. They said delivering on Meta’s vision “requires building the infrastructure that powers AI”.
What was the pledge?
In 2020, Meta set a goal of net-zero emissions across its entire value chain by 2030, in line with the Paris Agreement, which aims to hold long-term warming to 1.5C (2.7F) above pre-industrial levels.
Net zero means eliminating emissions as far as possible and buying credits from carbon removal projects to offset those that cannot be eliminated. The value chain covers emissions from sources such as purchased goods and services, as well as capital goods such as equipment, buildings and vehicles.
Data centres’ growing footprint
A study published this week in the journal Nature Sustainability found that 403 of the most powerful data centres in the United States accounted for about 2 percent of the country’s electricity use and a carbon footprint comparable to Denmark’s, the AFP news agency reported.
About 1,200 such “hyperscale” data centres are online, and hundreds more are planned. Globally, data centres used about 415 terawatt hours of electricity in 2024, about 1.5 percent of supply, and that could nearly double by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency.
A wider retreat
During US President Donald Trump’s second term, major American businesses have stepped back from environmental commitments.
The trend is not confined to Big Tech. General Motors, which set a goal of selling only zero-emission vehicles by 2035, backed the Trump administration’s weakening of a fuel economy rule this year.
Walmart acknowledged in 2024 that it would miss its first emissions target. Google, which pledged in 2020 to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, said this year that its emissions were still rising.
Coca-Cola and Pepsi have changed the baseline years for their emissions targets and weakened their ambitions.

items.text:
White House fires national cyber director over widespread outages
The White House fired national cyber director Sean Cairncross on Thursday following a week of technology disruptions affecting US air travel, email services and national security systems. The departure comes as the Trump administration faces criticism over its response to the outages, which officials say were unrelated incidents.
White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after tech outages hit US air travel, banking and national security systems.
Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.
Read more'Is this a cyberattack?' Grounded flights, a Microsoft outage and AI chaos fuel cybersecurity fears
"The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Cairncross declined to comment on his departure.
Technology-related outages have hit regularly over the last week, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services and a temporary disruption to the US National Security Agency's network.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The Trump administration has faced criticism over its response to the outages. The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions to critical systems over the past week were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.
Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

items.summary:
Democrats say law firm gave $11.8m in free services to Trump administration
Three top Democrats called Trump’s dealings with law firms a case of ‘official coercion’ and pledged investigations.
Democrats in the United States say their investigation has revealed that the law firm Kirkland & Ellis prov
items.text:
Democrats say law firm gave $11.8m in free services to Trump administration
Three top Democrats called Trump’s dealings with law firms a case of ‘official coercion’ and pledged investigations.
Democrats in the United States say their investigation has revealed that the law firm Kirkland & Ellis provided at least $11.8m in free legal work to President Donald Trump’s administration.
On Thursday, Representative Jamie Raskin, Senator Richard Blumenthal and Senator Adam Schiff released a statement calling the sum evidence of Trump’s “unprecedented official coercion of major law firms”.
Since Trump returned to the White House for a second term, he has issued executive orders seeking to bar certain law firms from receiving security clearances and government contracts.
His administration has also threatened law firms with workplace discrimination investigations. Those orders and probes have led some of the firms to enter into settlements with the Trump administration, offering millions of dollars in free services.
“We have recently received substantial and profoundly troubling information that this corrupt bargain went much further than originally understood,” the three Democrats said in the statement, citing the $11.8m in services.
They proceeded to request records from nine other law firms, in an effort to determine if they too had done free work on behalf of the Trump administration.
“Since April 2025, the lawmakers have repeatedly demanded answers about the ten firms’ dubious multimillion-dollar deals with President Trump,” the statement said.
“However, to date, the vast majority of the firms still have yet to provide any substantive answers or turn over a single responsive document.”
Midterm shift
The three Democrats involved in Thursday’s statement include lawmakers poised to take leadership roles in investigations during the upcoming 120th Congress.
The Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.
That will give the party power over Congress’s ability to oversee investigations and issue subpoenas. The new Congress is slated to be sworn in on January 3.
Raskin is currently the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee. Blumenthal, meanwhile, is the ranking member of the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.
Schiff, for his part, gained fame for leading Trump’s first impeachment trial in 2020, over allegations that the president abused his power by seeking Ukraine’s help for his first re-election bid. Trump has previously called for Schiff’s prosecution.
The three Democrats say they received information about Kirkland & Ellis’s free services for the Trump administration two days after the midterm race.
Some $4m in services was reportedly offered to the Department of Commerce. Another $2.2m went to the Department of Defense, and $1.6m was dedicated to the US Postal Service.
Kirkland & Ellis also reportedly gave $2m in services to the US International Development Finance Corporation, an agency that provides loans and development assistance to overseas projects.
The Democrats also said $1.8m went to an “investment entity negotiated between the Trump Administration and Japan to create a $550 billion slush fund”.
Law firms cut deals
In 2025, Kirkland & Ellis agreed to settle with the Trump administration after the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) opened an investigation into the law firm’s employment practices.
It accused Kirkland & Ellis of embracing diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), a slogan for building greater opportunities for under-represented groups in education and the workplace.
The Trump administration, however, has characterised DEI as illegal discrimination, disadvantaging men and white people.
“The EEOC is prepared to root out discrimination anywhere it may rear its head, including in our nation’s elite law firms,” the commission’s acting chair said at the time.
In a Truth Social post on April 11, 2025, Trump revealed that Kirkland & Ellis had pledged $125m in free services. He also indicated that the EEOC would halt its investigation as a result.
Other law firms likewise entered into agreements to avoid the consequences of Trump’s executive actions or employment-related probes.
Estimates indicate that they collectively pledged nearly $1bn in pro bono services.
The handful of law firms that fought Trump’s executive orders, however, won their cases, with judges ruling the president’s actions to be unconstitutional.
In the case involving the law firm Perkins Coie, Judge Beryl Howell said the executive order against it was an “overt attempt to suppress and punish certain viewpoints”.
Fears of corruption
The Democrats in Thursday’s statement highlighted other concerns with the agreements.
The deals, they said, were announced on Truth Social, Trump’s social media platform. That made “the President the sole judge of whether those firms were complying with their obligations – putting these firms at the political mercy of the Administration”.
The Democrats also warned that law firms like Kirkland & Ellis might be dissuaded from taking on certain clients, for fear of upsetting Trump.
“For people and communities who rely on pro bono lawyers to defend their rights, that could mean facing the full power and intensifying fury of the federal government alone,” they said.
In a November letter obtained by the Reuters news agency, Kirkland said it began negotiating with the Trump administration after rival firm Skadden reached its own deal in March 2025.
It added that its White House agreement has had “little impact” on its pro bono work, telling lawmakers that the firm “still devotes substantial pro bono resources to interests that could be considered ‘progressive'”.
The law firm is represented by prominent Washington litigator Beth Wilkinson of Wilkinson Stekloff. She did not immediately respond to Reuters’s request for comment.

items.text:
‘Completely messed up everything’: Malawi’s fuel crisis causes chaos
Motorists and businesses struggle as shortages disrupt daily life.
Blantyre, Malawi – Finding fuel in Malawi has become a daily struggle, with motorists spending hours, sometimes entire nights, waiting for tankers that may never arrive.
As shortages persist, filling stations across the country have become flashpoints for frustration and violence as motorists compete for dwindling supplies.
Ken Mhango, 40, a car flipper in Blantyre, recently drove to a nearby filling station after a friend told him a fuel tanker was on its way. He had gone several days without fuel.
Twelve people were already waiting when he arrived, but the situation soon turned chaotic.
“Minibus drivers and motorcycle taxi operators started arriving and jumping queues. They were so reckless they didn’t care if they bumped your vehicle. A scuffle erupted and I saw others, especially women, desperately trying to keep their place in the queue. It took me four hours to get 20 litres but others spent the night in the queue,” he told Al Jazeera.
Violence at filling stations
The scramble for petrol has increasingly turned violent in Malawi’s cities and towns. Although the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority publishes daily schedules indicating which filling stations are expected to receive fuel, motorists say uncertainty over deliveries makes it difficult to plan their journeys.
Videos of confrontations have circulated on social media, including footage appearing to show people attacking a man at a filling station. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The mayor of Blantyre has also been sued for assault following an incident at a fuel queue, while an attendant was killed after being struck by a vehicle during a commotion at a filling station, according to local media reports.
Purchases are reportedly rationed to 20 litres (5.3 gallons) a day, while motorists sometimes pay attendants for an additional five litres, Mhango said.
“The whole chaos that this has created is hectic. It is very hectic and it has created an atmosphere of uncertainty. This is happening when money is scarce, you have to make sure that you plan properly to survive,” he said.
On another occasion, Mhango arrived at Nyabadwe filling station in Blantyre at 5pm after joining a convoy of motorists searching for fuel. The tanker arrived at 9pm, and did not leave until 1am.
“My schedule has been completely altered. Now commuting is no longer a norm but a luxury. I have two parcels in town but I can’t even manage to go and get them,” he said.
Unable to find sufficient supplies at filling stations, Mhango turned to the black market. He paid 30,000 Malawian kwacha (about $17.31) for two litres of petrol for his father. On another occasion, he suspected fuel bought for his garage had been mixed with water after an engine malfunctioned.
“The crisis has completely changed and messed up everything. As a businessperson who deals with vehicles at my garage, people are no longer bringing their vehicles any more because of lack of fuel. And we can’t take our equipment to follow the client,” he said.
He added that his business was unlikely to meet its monthly targets, forcing him to consider docking the salaries of employees who assist him.
Black market dangers
Selling fuel without the required permits is illegal in Malawi, but shortages have created opportunities for vendors to sell petrol at inflated prices.
Motorists who need to travel for work, business or medical care are increasingly turning to informal sellers despite the high prices and safety risks.
According to GlobalPetrolPrices, petrol in Malawi costs about $3.24 per litre, more than double the global average of approximately $1.52.
The informal trade has also proved deadly. Authorities have stepped up arrests of illegal vendors, while fires and explosions caused by unsafe fuel storage have killed people.
Earlier this year, petrol vendors and motorcycle taxi operators protested in Lilongwe after a suspected black market fuel seller was burned alive in an explosion following a police chase, local media reported.
Malawi’s Nation newspaper has documented at least six deaths from fuel explosions this year, including incidents involving families and children.
Calls for accountability
The shortages, alongside foreign-exchange problems and electricity blackouts, have fuelled demands for government accountability.
The Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC) planned nationwide demonstrations on November 17, calling for the resignation of the energy minister over persistent fuel shortages and power cuts.
The protests were postponed after police said they could not provide adequate security because officers were committed to a governing-party parade scheduled for the same day.
Michael Kaiyatsa, HRDC chairperson, told Al Jazeera that the decision reflected “genuine concerns about public safety”, rather than a retreat from the coalition’s demands.
He described the fuel situation as “heartbreaking”, saying its effects extended beyond transport and commerce to people’s access to essential services.
“It affects access to healthcare, education, food, employment and other essential services; ultimately this is a human rights issue,” he said.
“People are struggling to get their children to school. We have small-scale businesses that are losing money. We have employees that are failing to get to work, and ordinary motorists that are spending hours and sometimes entire days just looking for fuel.”
Kaiyatsa said the shortages were pushing people to buy fuel on the black market, not necessarily because they wanted to break the law but because they were trying to meet their daily needs.
“We must therefore be clear that this is the responsibility of the government to ensure that fuel is normalised,” he said.
While acknowledging the dangers of illegal fuel trading, he said law enforcement must respect human rights and due pr

"Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her
items.text:
Cincinnati's famous hippo Fiona dies after eating visitor's hat
November 20, 2026
Fiona the hippo has died at the Cincinnati Zoo in the US after swallowing a visitor's hat which was accidentally thrown into her enclosure. She was nine years old.
"Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome," the zoo said. "The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover."
Fiona was born in 2017 prematurely, with the hippo becoming a social media sensation. At the time of her birth, she only weighed 29 pounds (13 kilograms) and was in a fight to survive.
Social media users watched Fiona's daily activities as grew up. She was named after the character in the "Shrek" film series.
US second lady Usha Vance, Ohio Governor-Elect Acton remember Fiona
Fiona's death was met with reactions from her fans and political leaders.
Second lady Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of their kids face-to-face with Fiona at her enclosure.
"We are so sad to hear the news about Fiona," Vance said. Vice President Vance hails from the greater Cincinnati area and the US second family has a home there.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval lauded Fiona as "a symbol of perservance and joy" in the city.
Ohio Governor-Elect Amy Acton said: "Fiona captured the hearts of millions and became one of Cincinnati's most beloved icons."
"Her story brought joy, hope and a little extra magic to our state," Acton added.

items.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
items.summary:
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.
The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering
items.text:
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.
The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”
“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”
The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”
TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.
Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.
Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.
The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”
Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”

items.text:
More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
- Published
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.
While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.
These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.
"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."
The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.
"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.
Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.
"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.
- 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted 
  - Published11 November
- A really simple guide to climate change 
  - Published6 November
Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.
The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.
Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.
Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.
But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?
"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.
"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."
Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.
"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.

European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prim
items.text:
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
- Published
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.
- Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance 
  - Published14 hours ago
"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.
He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity."
"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying: "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."
Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.
The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.
There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.
But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.
It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.

items.summary:
PM Sánchez admits 'mistakes' in key debate ahead of Spain's election
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez acknowledged shortcomings in his government on Thursday as he faced conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo in the campaign's only televised debate. The November 29 election could leave the far-
items.text:
PM Sánchez admits 'mistakes' in key debate ahead of Spain's election
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez acknowledged shortcomings in his government on Thursday as he faced conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo in the campaign's only televised debate. The November 29 election could leave the far-right Vox party in a position to enter government.
Spain's Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez acknowledged making "mistakes" as he faced off with his main conservative rival in a key debate on Thursday before an election next week that could leave the far right on the cusp of power.
The pair clashed over the economy, housing, immigration, corruption, foreign policy, as well as policies towards women, repeatedly interrupting each other during the live televised showdown.
"My government has not been perfect, I have made mistakes. But I am also fully aware that we have always governed in the right direction," Sanchez said at the outset.
Pointing to economic growth and employment figures, he argued Spain was in better shape than when he took power in 2018, a claim rejected by the leader of the mainstream right-wing Popular Party (PP), Alberto Nunez Feijoo.
"Having a job does not guarantee you can make ends meet. Having a job does not guarantee you can afford a home either. You have crushed the middle class," he told Sanchez.
Read moreSpain's right holds poll lead over Sanchez's Socialists ahead of November 29 snap election
"The Spanish economy is posting growth figures, but many families are still having to perform financial gymnastics to make ends meet."
Feijoo rattled off what he called the government's failures, including soaring prices, high taxes and a housing crisis.
- Graft cases -
A darling of the international left for his clashes with US President Donald Trump and Israel, Sanchez has become a polarising figure in Spain following eight years in power.
His Socialists trail in most polls to the PP, which is predicted to win the most seats on November 29 but without securing a majority.
That scenario could hand a decisive role to the ascendant far-right party Vox, the third-largest force in parliament which has already governed with the PP at the regional level.
Further complicating the situation for Sanchez is the weakness of other leftist parties whose support proved crucial to keep him in power after the last general election in 2023.

The PP won more seats in that vote, but Sanchez unexpectedly cut the gap in polling and stayed in power after cobbling together a motley alliance with left-wing and regional separatist parties.
Sanchez, who has made escaping seemingly hopeless positions a hallmark of his career, believes he can defy the predictions again.
He has sought to capitalise on anger over Spain's housing crisis, which brought forward an election originally due in 2027 after the right voted down the government's measures for tenants.
But Feijoo accused Sanchez of not doing enough to avoid the housing crunch and brought up corruption scandals that have affected his relatives and senior Socialists.
He also blamed Sanchez's government for two high-speed train collisions this year that together killed 115 people.
"Spain deserves a respectable prime minister, and (Pedro Sanchez) is not one," Feijoo said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

'Problem for Europe'
Sanchez warned a PP-Vox coalition would roll back hard-won social rights and economic gains.
"We can do even better, because we will deliver greater social justice, better public services and greater prosperity," Sanchez said.
He also defended his government's more liberal approach to immigration, bucking a broader European trend towards tougher migration controls and stricter asylum policies.
In April, Spain approved a plan to grant legal status to hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants already living in the country, provided they meet residency and other requirements.
Read moreKing Felipe VI says Ceuta is ‘inalienable’ part of Spain in landmark visit
"You are a problem for Europe when it comes to immigration," his rival retorted, recalling the migrant rush into the Spanish city of Ceuta on the northern coast of Africa in July.
The debate was the campaign's only head-to-head encounter between the two main contenders.
Vox leader Santiago Abascal, who could take the far right into power for the first time since the end of General Francisco Franco's dictatorship in 1975, has dismissed the match-up.
"I don't know what they will debate tonight. I am the one who is missing for there to be a real difference of opinions," he said earlier.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
items.summary:
Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.
At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocke
items.text:
Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.
At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.
Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.
However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”
With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.
$104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.
Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.
Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.
28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.
The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says.
More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.
Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.
All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

items.summary:
El Salvador’s Bukele expected to formalise bid for third presidential term
The Salvadoran president has won popularity at home and abroad through a crime crackdown that has granted the state enormous power.
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele is set to formally register his candidacy for his country’s
items.text:
El Salvador’s Bukele expected to formalise bid for third presidential term
The Salvadoran president has won popularity at home and abroad through a crime crackdown that has granted the state enormous power.
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele is set to formally register his candidacy for his country’s upcoming presidential race, as he seeks a third consecutive term.
Thursday was the registration deadline for the election, which is slated for February 28, 2027.
The 45-year-old president has been widely expected to seek re-election, a move that would further consolidate his party’s leadership in the Central American country.
Bukele is the founder and leader of the Nuevas Ideas party, which controls El Salvador’s Legislative Assembly by a wide margin.
While El Salvador’s constitution previously prohibited presidents from seeking immediate re-election, the Supreme Court overturned that rule in 2021, paving the way for Bukele to run for a second term in 2024.
Then, in 2025, the Legislative Assembly passed a constitutional amendment allowing Bukele to seek a third term. The amendment also extended the length of a presidential term from five to six years.
Bukele secured his party’s nomination for the 2027 race in July. He is expected to return to the ballot alongside his current vice president, Felix Ulloa.
Bukele’s time in office has been defined by a crackdown on criminal gangs that has won him massive popularity at home and turned him into an icon for the political right across Latin America.
In 2022, his government announced a so-called state of emergency to address high levels of crime in the country.
It empowered the police to make sweeping arrests, but it also heralded the suspension of key civil liberties. Some people were detained without charge. Mass trials have been carried out, with hundreds of defendants being sentenced at a time.
More than 1 percent of the country’s population is estimated to have been arrested as a result, with little due process for those seeking to contest their guilt, according to human rights groups.
Advocates also warn that rights abuses, torture and poor conditions are systematic in Salvadoran prisons.
The state of emergency has been extended for years, although it was initially intended as a temporary measure and the government claims El Salvador’s gangs have been all but dismantled.
The United States Treasury has also accused Bukele’s government of negotiating with the gangs in secret, offering incentives to help lower crime.
But experts say human rights activists and members of the news media have seen their ability to monitor abuses and corruption in the country hampered under Bukele.
Some, like human rights lawyer Ruth Lopez, have allegedly been detained for their work without access to legal support. She has spent more than a year in “incommunicado detention”, according to the group Amnesty International.
Under Bukele, El Salvador has also passed a Foreign Agents Law that allows the government to restrict civil society groups that receive funding from abroad.
Those efforts have prompted allegations that Bukele has weaponised the state against his critics.
But those concerns have done little to dent his popularity, and Bukele is considered the clear favourite to win the election.
A handful of candidates, including Maytee Iraheta of the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance and Rafael Aguirre of the left-wing Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front, are also set to contest the presidency.

items.summary:

items.text:
'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
- Published
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.
They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.
On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.
Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.
"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.
More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.
In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.
An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.
Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.
The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."
Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.
They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.
He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".
If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.
"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.
It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.
"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."
He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.
On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.
He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.
The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.
What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.
He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

items.title: Four bodies recovered after Senegal boat capsizes amid migration surge
items.summary:
Four bodies recovered after Senegal boat capsizes amid migration surge
Four bodies have been recovered after a migrant boat capsized off Senegal’s coast, as authorities continue searching for survivors amid fears that the death toll could rise significantly.
Boubacar Seye, president of the nonprofit
items.text:
Four bodies recovered after Senegal boat capsizes amid migration surge
Four bodies have been recovered after a migrant boat capsized off Senegal’s coast, as authorities continue searching for survivors amid fears that the death toll could rise significantly.
Boubacar Seye, president of the nonprofit Horizons Sans Frontieres, confirmed the latest death toll to the Reuters news agency on Thursday, a day after the vessel capsized near the coastal town of Yenne, south of Dakar.
A local official said at least 50 people were aboard the boat, which struck a rock while migrants were being transferred from smaller fishing vessels to a larger wooden pirogue.
The number of people still missing remains unclear.
Canary Islands
The incident comes amid an intensifying wave of attempted Atlantic crossings from West Africa to Spain’s Canary Islands, with migrant boats being intercepted or rescued almost daily.
New figures from Spain’s Interior Ministry show that 24,364 migrants reached the Canary Islands between January 1 and November 15, compared with 14,690 during the same period last year, an increase of nearly two-thirds.
The ministry had recorded just 13,327 arrivals by the end of October, meaning 11,037 people reached the archipelago in the first 15 days of November alone.
The surge has persisted despite extensive maritime operations. Senegal’s navy said it had rescued or intercepted 1,424 people on November 16 and 17, including passengers aboard nine fishing boats, according to the Senegalese Press Agency (APS).
Cheikh Sadibou Senghor, head of Senegal’s National Division for Combating Migrant Smuggling, said authorities had intercepted 6,889 people in operations linked to irregular migration, prevented 107 departures and dismantled 88 smuggling networks between January and November, APS reported.
Just days before the boat capsized, authorities announced the dismantling of a suspected migrant-smuggling network in Yenne itself, arresting 14 people and seizing two boats, three engines and 12.5 million CFA francs ($22,000), according to APS.
Nearly 600 dead
The United Nations refugee agency said nearly 600 people had died trying to reach the Canary Islands from West Africa so far this year, highlighting the dangers of the increasingly busy migration route.
As authorities struggle to contain the surge, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has called for greater efforts to improve employment opportunities for young people.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Faye requested a detailed assessment of the challenges facing efforts to curb irregular migration, according to a government statement cited by Reuters.
But Seye warned that tougher enforcement measures alone would not prevent further tragedies.
“We need to wake up to the gravity of the situation. The strategy deployed until now is not working,” he told Reuters.
“We need to fix the root causes of this problem.”

items.text:
After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those games. Their current run of 17 successive league wins against Fulham is the longest run of victories by one club against a single opponent in English top-flight history. It is a reflection of the changing realities of English football, and the gulf that has opened between the teams that dominate it and those who seek to challenge them, that of the top 10 such runs all but one occurred in whole or in part after 2010 and six of them have been achieved by Sheikh Mansour’s Manchester City, with Chelsea responsible for another two, Manchester United one, and Portsmouth’s postwar, 13-game supremacy over Everton – a wild ride that included two 5-0s, a 5-1, a 6-3 and a 7-0 – the anomaly. Simon Burnton
Positivity surrounds Aston Villa despite them failing to win in four matches, the last of which ended in agonising fashion; they had to settle for a 4-4 draw at Manchester United after twice squandering a two-goal advantage. Villa should have managed the final minutes better, but a home date with Sunderland presents an opportunity to return to winning ways. Unai Emery needs to eliminate the defensive naivety that has blighted some performances and the expected absence of Matty Cash, this time owing to concussion sustained on Poland duty, would deny the Villa manager his preferred defensive lineup. This fixture threw up a classic last season, Tammy Abraham scoring a stoppage-time winner to extend the visitors’ miserable record at Villa Park. Sunderland have won on only two of their past 17 league visits, their last victory coming in 2011 courtesy of the former Villa loanee Phil Bardsley. Ben Fisher
The last time Alex Scott played for Bournemouth, Marco Rose was yet to taste victory in the Premier League. When the 23-year-old returns to midfield he will do so with the team in a totally different place. Bournemouth have racked up eight straight wins in all competitions before hosting Nottingham Forest on Saturday and Scott, who has been able to build his fitness during the international break after a thigh problem, may have to wait his turn owing to the form of Tyler Adams and Ryan Christie. If Rose opts for momentum, then Eli Junior Kroupi, fresh from scoring his first France goal, could make his first start of the season after sustaining a freak foot injury in pre-season. Bournemouth have hardly been short of firepower, though, with Evanilson scoring seven goals in his past eight games. BF
Chelsea left Wearside battered and bruised after being pushed around by Brian Brobbey. The Sunderland forward bullied Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill, who had to be substituted at half-time, and won the game’s decisive penalty with a solo run that left Xabi Alonso angry with his side’s powderpuff defending. Alonso insisted Chelsea had prepared for Brobbey’s threat; the Chelsea manager will hope they are better at putting the plan into practice when they face another target man on Saturday. Leeds head to Stamford Bridge and will look to Dominic Calvert-Lewin, fresh from helping England get over the line against Spain last weekend, to unnerve Alonso’s defenders. Jacob Steinberg
Thomas Frank’s first assessment of his new charges after taking over at Crystal Palace this week included the nuggets that “we’re conceding too many goals … we need to work on the defensive side of things with principles, attitude, everything regarding that”, and in particular “we need to work on the set pieces, that’s key”. If he can’t inspire an immediate improvement this is where this match could be decided, being as it is an encounter between the league’s worst set-piece defenders – no one comes close to the 67 shots and xG of 7.44 coughed up by Palace at restarts – and the best. Though Coventry have let in one goal from set pieces, and neither Brentford nor Liverpool have shipped any, the hosts’ set-piece xG of 1.65 is a league low, and they were equally outstanding from dead-ball situations in the Championship last season. The home side will be boosted by the return of the 6ft 4in defender Bobby Thomas, who, despite a calf injury that meant he missed the last two games and the final third of the one before that, has still made more clearances than any other Coventry player. SB
It may have been a slightly strange week for Tottenham fans. They have watched as their former managers Mauricio Pochettino and Thomas Frank have been installed at Manchester United and Crystal Palace respectively, while their current head coach, Roberto De Zerbi, picked up the Premier League’s manager of the month award for October. That is reflective of the improvement De Zerbi has overseen in recent weeks, with Spurs happy to move forward with the Italian and avoid the chaos enveloping some of their rivals. The long-held assumption among some connected to Tottenham that Pochettino would one day return to save the club must now be banished; De Zerbi needs full buy-in from everyone to build his project. That’s the only way Spurs can ensure they steer clear of future crises. Dominic Booth
With the temperature in Newcastle forecast to dip to 0C at kick-off, Matthias Jaissle is perhaps hoping that his team’s guests from north London (where a balmy 9C is predicted at 5.30pm) freeze in the Tyneside chill. Otherwise it is hard to envisage his young side overcoming a formidable looking Arsenal on a day when Newcastle’s head coach seeks what would be only his second win in seven games. Home fans will not merely be hurt by the sight of their much-missed former captain Bruno Guimarães wearing Arsenal colours but decidedly nervous about a fixture that precedes a run of tricky engagements involving a trip to Brighton and home dates with Manchester United and Sunderland. Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level
- Published
