That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across t
items.text:
Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level
- Published
It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.
That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across their opening 15 matches of the season, but also the elite teams in Europe seem to have gone up another level.
In the space of seven days, Arsenal have witnessed first hand what it takes to reach those heights - and the gap they must bridge.
Last week, they were resilient at Barcelona to earn a very respectable 1-1 draw, but were fortunate the Spanish side were not clinical with their chances at Camp Nou.
On Thursday night, they were outplayed at home in losing 2-0 to an excellent Lyon side, who look on course to match or better their runner-up finish from last season.
One point from such games could be pleasing - but that only shows the work Arsenal need to do to be considered one of the top teams in Europe.
Lyon superior in every department
Arsenal came into Thursday's defeat by Lyon off the back of a fifth successive Women's Super League draw at Emirates Stadium against London City Lionesses.
In contrast, Lyon have been flying domestically, winning all nine of their matches, scoring 49 goals, and then not conceding any in their unbeaten Champions League run.
Such form sets the pace and it was clear at Meadow Park that they were superior to Arsenal in every department.
Vibrant Germany international Jule Brand gave them the lead midway through the first half and Melchie Dumornay sealed the win with a powerful strike in the 57th minute.
Arsenal defender Leah Williamson said the "better team won the game" and manager Renee Slegers highlighted the difference in physicality between the teams.
"Compared to last year when we played Lyon [in the semi-finals], they are even better now. They have standout individual quality," Slegers said.
"They dominated in the first half. We had solutions for the second half and had more presence. We wore them down better but it still didn't lead to open chances."
Lyon had a 3.33 expected goals ratio on Thursday, serving up 23 shots to Arsenal's seven. They created six big chances and 14 of their shots were inside the box.
Dumornay oozed quality, midfielder Lily Yohannes showed composure and Brand was very impressive both defensively and going forward for Lyon, deployed in a new position.
Those individuals have benefitted from the expertise of former Barcelona manager Jonatan Giraldez, who joined in June 2025 - the month after Arsenal won the Champions League - and has now had the time he needed to impose his style.
As a result, Lyon have gone up another level and the gap between these two teams has widened by Arsenal's drop-off this season.
Slegers also said Arsenal had "prepared all we could" for the intensity that Lyon brought in London - but it still did not have an impact.
Asked how far off Lyon they currently are, Slegers said: "It's 2-0 today and they are better than us but it doesn't mean if we were to play them again soon, this season, that it would be the same game again.
"We saw moments where we did well and we know from the last couple of years we can hurt Lyon.
"But for today, their pace and physicality helped them get too much dominance in the game and that is one of their strengths. Then it became hard for us."
Williamson 'aware of where the gaps are'
Williamson said Arsenal "know what they need to do to be better" and that they are aware of "where the gaps are" to Europe's elite.
They are already 12 points off the pace in the Women's Super League title race and are unlikely to qualify automatically for the Champions League quarter-finals.
"The level rises year on year. Everybody cops goals - we have to try not to and we have to create," said Williamson following the defeat by Lyon.
"We're all focused and we're all together. That's the most comforting thing for me - but this has been a tough period."
It has not all been bad despite disappointing results - and context is important.
Over a gruelling seven days, they have faced European holders Barcelona, WSL high-flyers London City Lionesses and record Champions League winners Lyon.
They showed grit and resilience out in Barcelona last week - traits that have not been on show enough for Arsenal this season, but are clearly there.
Players like Williamson, striker Alessia Russo and summer signings Georgia Stanway and Ona Batlle know what it takes to compete at the highest level.
Arsenal invested in the summer transfer window and brought in proven, experienced players, but that has not translated into results - yet.
Giraldez said time with his players has helped improve Lyon and perhaps that is what Arsenal need - patience.
"I think they are changing now. They made a good game against Barcelona and it's very difficult to go there and get a point," said Giraldez.
"The game against London City was much better. It's not just about them, but also about us. Now we have improved and play better football than last year.
"I think it is a matter of time [for Arsenal]. They have a good coach and good players. In general, they have all the ingredients to have a good season."

items.text:
Price tag for US war in Iran barrels past $48 billion
November 20, 2026
The cost of the US war in Iran, which Donald Trump launched without Congressional approval on February 28, blew past $48.3 billion (€44 billion) on November 13, according to Pentagon budgetary official Arthur Miller.
Miller laid out the figures during Thursday testimony before the US Senate Armed Services Committee as his nomination to become Navy comptroller is considered.
Miller said the costs cover US military operations, equipment and munitions but not damage sustained at US military installations across the Middle East.
How much damage has Iran inflicted on US military installations in the Middle East?
According to news agency AP, damage to hundreds of aircraft hangars, barracks, radar systems, warehouses and other US military infrastructure has run up into the billions of dollars, however, Miller failed to provide an estimate of the total cost when pressed during the hearing.
Committee Chairman Roger Wicker, a Republican from Mississippi, called on Miller to provide the figures as soon as possible.
In October, the Wall Street Journal cited Pentagon sources who said damage to US facilities in the region could range from $5 billion to as much as $15 billion.
The Washington-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies put the cost for repairing buildings alone — excluding equipment and systems inside — at more than $4 billion.
A war by any name, is still a very expensive undertaking
The Trump administration has variously argued that the war is not a war, that it has been won, and that it will be over soon. There is currently no end in sight and on top of the US military's costs, the global economy is getting pummeled every day as a result of the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz — which is the direct result of US attacks on the Islamic Republic.
The Trump administration is calling on Congress to pass the Pentagon's $1.5 trillion 2027 defense budget — a 40% increase over 2026 — in order to fund America's military. Unlikely prior to the November 3 midterm elections, the prospects of that figure being approved now that Democrats have taken control of both houses of Congress from Republicans would seem nigh impossible.

items.text:
New Ukraine talks including Europe to be held 'soon' — Merz
November 20, 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Friday he believes new talks regarding Russia's invasion of Ukraine with European leaders taking part will occur "soon."
What did Merz say about the next Ukraine talks?
"Of course we are prepared to hold talks with Russia, we have always said this. These talks are now set to take place soon," Merz said after a meeting of Ukraine's allies in Berlin. He did not give a concrete date for the next talks, but said Europe's interests would be represented by Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was present at the Coalition of the Willing summit in the German capital, along with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff.
Merz said the talks including Europe would take place on "neutral ground," such as the United Arab Emirates.
Merz along with other European leaders have been critical of meetings between US, Ukrainian and Russian representatives regarding the conflict, arguing that Europe needs a direct seat at the negotiating table.
Putin, in talks with Trump, says European leaders invited to Moscow
Russia's invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, with the Trump administration prioritizing an end to the war.
Trump took part in a bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Friday, with Trump saying the two leaders would discuss the war in closed-door talks. Putin acknowledged that Europeans want a seat at the table, and said Russia invited European leaders to Moscow.
"We understand that discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without Europeans," Putin said, while rejecting any military cooperation between Europe and Ukraine.
Merz: 'Yalta format cannot bring peace' to Ukraine
Trump also took part in a historic trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The Trump-Putin-Xi meeting raised fears that the US, Russia and China are looking to carve up the world into spheres of influence. It drew comparisons with the February 1945 Yalta Conference, where US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Union leader Joseph Stalin discussed Europe's future as Nazi Germany's defeat was imminent in World War II.
Following the Trump-Xi-Putin summit, Merz said a "Yalta format cannot bring peace" to Ukraine. He downplayed the Shenzhen summit between the three leaders as a "photo opportunity."
Merz handed out pieces of the Berlin Wall to leaders at the Coalition of the Willing summit, saying the Yalta structure had brought "oppression, insecurity and a lack of peace."
"This is exactly what Yalta stood for," Merz said.
The Yalta format sought to divide post-war Germany into four zones: US, UK, France and the USSR. This later led to the construction of the Berlin Wall dividing the city into West and East Berlin, with city residents attempting to cross the barrier shot dead by border guards.

items.text:
Trump posthumously pardons US baseball legend Pete Rose
- Published
US President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose.
"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.
Rose, who died in 2024 at the age of 83, pleaded guilty in 1990 to two counts of filing false tax returns. He was also given a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball (MLB) after an investigation revealed he bet on games.
The baseball star was posthumously reinstated to MLB, in which he played for 24 seasons, last year and made eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame.
Trump also said on Thursday that Rose's "record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken".
In fact, Rose accumulated a record 4,256 hits - which MLB defines as a batter striking the baseball into fair territory and reaching base without doing so via an error or a fielder's choice - during his career, which is more than any other player. He played a total of 3,562 games.
According to Trump, Rose "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess".
The BBC has contacted the Baseball Hall of Fame for comment.
The US president had previously floated the idea of pardoning Rose in March last year before the MLB reinstated him.
"Major League Baseball didn't have the courage or decency to put the late, great, Pete Rose, also known as 'Charlie Hustle,' into the Baseball Hall of fame," he wrote on Truth Social at the time.
"Now he is dead, will never experience the thrill of being selected, even though he was a FAR BETTER PLAYER than most of those who made it, and can only be named posthumously. WHAT A SHAME," Trump added.
MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred issued a decision in May 2025 that created a pathway for Rose to be eligible to be inducted into the baseball Hall of Fame - a ruling that also applied to 16 other people - as early as 2028.
In August 1989, Rose agreed to the permanent ban from the sport after MLB investigators found that he bet on his team, the Cincinnati Reds, multiple times while he was playing on and managing the team from 1985 to 1987.
In July 1990, after Rose admitted to failing to report $354,968 (£271,107) in income over a four-year period, he was sentenced to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform community service at the time.

items.summary:
Six killed in suspected gas explosion at Georgia apartment building

Six people, including a child, have been killed after a suspected natural gas explosion caused part of a five-storey apartment building to collapse
items.text:
Six killed in suspected gas explosion at Georgia apartment building
Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said authorities would temporarily relocate 28 families.
Six people, including a child, have been killed after a suspected natural gas explosion caused part of a five-storey apartment building to collapse in Georgia’s capital, Tbilisi, according to the AFP news agency.
The blast struck the residential building in the suburban Ponichala district on Thursday morning, trapping several residents beneath the rubble.
Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili said rescuers had recovered six bodies from the wreckage, including that of a young child.
A three-year-old girl was pulled alive from the rubble after several hours of rescue operations, prompting applause from onlookers gathered at the scene.
Emergency Management Service chief Teimuraz Mgebrishvili said one of the women found dead was believed to be the girl’s mother, according to AFP.
Doctors at Ingorokva University Clinic said the rescued girl was in stable condition and scans had revealed no serious traumatic injuries, Georgian Public Broadcaster (1TV) reported.
An 11-year-old boy was also being treated in intensive care, although his condition was described as relatively stable, according to the broadcaster.
Tamazashvili said preliminary findings indicated that the explosion occurred on the fifth floor when a resident attempted to switch on a gas heater.
However, gas supplier Tbilisi Energy said the apartment identified as the likely source of the explosion had been registered as unoccupied and had recorded no gas consumption over the past year, according to 1TV. The company said it had not yet been able to inspect the damaged property.
Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said authorities would temporarily relocate 28 families, comprising more than 100 residents, to hotels after structural assessments found two sections of the building unsafe, according to Georgia’s Interpressnews agency.
Prosecutor Levan Vepkhvadze said a criminal investigation had been launched into possible violations of safety regulations.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney gener
items.text:
California probing whether China improperly acquired Nvidia technology
- Published
California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.
The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.
Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.
Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

items.text:
Judge finds Thomas Markle mentally fit to stand trial on child abuse charges
- Published
A judge in Florida has declared Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, to be mentally competent to stand trial for possessing indecent images of children.
The hearing came after an evaluation by a court-appointed psychiatrist conducted on Prince Harry's 82-year-old father-in-law.
Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was ordered to stay in jail pending trial earlier this month after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.
The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home that specialises in dementia. His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles uncovered the abuse material.
Markle appeared in court in Tampa in a wheelchair, and his lawyers did not dispute the court-appointed psychiatrist's finding that he is mentally competent to understand the nature and consequences of the charge against him.
His next court hearing is scheduled for early December, but any trial is expected to take place in California, where the federal charge was filed.
Inside the storage units in Los Angeles the FBI says agents found about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades.
Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".
He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.
On Monday, police in the Philippines asked prosecutors to charge Markle with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.
Last month, police there obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018, and he did not attend her wedding in London that same year.
The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic
items.text:
Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.
Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services.
An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.
Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.
“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”
With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

items.text:
Major anti-gang offensive in Haiti kills 34 suspected gang members
Haitian security forces launched a major offensive on Thursday to retake Martissant, a strategic corridor linking Port-au-Prince with the country's western and southern regions that gangs have controlled for five years. Police said at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in clashes involving a private security task force.
Armed forces in Haiti launched an aggressive operation on Thursday to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions.
It is the first significant operation in the five years since violent gangs seized control of Martissant, located in the western tip of Port-au-Prince.
Haiti’s National Police posted a video on X stating that at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in Martissant during a fight with police officers working with a task force composed of members from Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former US Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince.
Local media reported heavy gunfire and explosive drones in the area as Haiti’s police posted a video of armoured vehicles rumbling through the community.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Martissant is located along Route 2, the main road that leads out of Port-au-Prince to important western and southern cities. Thousands of people would travel through Martissant every day before gangs seized control of the area more than five years ago, disrupting the country’s economy as they prevented goods from entering or leaving the capital. Gangs have since charged tolls or randomly opened fire on cars or buses that dare cross through.
Ever since gangs seized absolute control of Martissant, aid workers and Haitian civilians have been forced to take alternative transportation or use rural back roads.
The fight to control Martissant began in June 2021, when gangs from Grand-Ravine and Village-de-Dieu attacked the Ti-Bois gang. Armed men set fire to homes, killed families, destroyed businesses and seized control of Martissant’s police station.
The clashes forced at least 19,000 people to flee their homes and affected some 800,000 people overall, according to a July 2022 United Nations report.
Several years ago, gangs operating between Tabarre and Carrefour would demand some $380 from those transiting through Martissant, according to a 2023 UN report.
Read moreHaitians rally behind Bukele as Salvadoran troops battle gangs
Last year, Haiti’s Center for Analysis and Research in Human Rights noted that ever since Martissant fell, hundreds of public and private institutions were relocated and more than one million people were forced to flee their homes.
As the fight in Martissant continues, a UN-backed gang suppression force also has made recent inroads against gangs in a push to not only displace them but prevent their return.
“Operations are entering a new phase: increasing pressure on gang networks, dismantling more strongholds, and extending control over strategic areas,” the force wrote Thursday on X.
The gang suppression force said it’s working in places including Tabarre in Port-au-Prince and in Haiti’s central Artibonite region, which has come under repeated violent attacks by armed men.
The force said it has come under fire as it advances along Route 5, “removing obstacles established by gangs to isolate communities and control key routes.”
Read moreHaitian police retake national stadium after two years of gang control
The force said it also cleared and secured a church and school that gangs had been controlling north of Gros-Morne.
“It is about restoring freedom of movement, reopening access to public institutions, and re-establishing State presence for communities that have endured years of gang control,” the force wrote Sunday on X.
Also fighting gangs are some 2,500 troops deployed by El Salvador last month when four of their own went missing after an October 18 attack in Haiti’s capital.
Following orders by Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, the troops have attacked the main homes of two of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders, Jeff and Lanmò San Jou, this month. Neither one was killed.
Read moreAmnesty urges El Salvador to disclose terms of Haiti troop deployment
Thousands of Haitians poured into the streets of Port-au-Prince and beyond this week in support of Bukele, but experts have criticised the unilateral operations of Salvadoran troops and noted that the use of explosive drones has claimed a growing number of innocent victims.
A small group of Salvadorans are separately working with the gang suppression force.
In late September, El Salvador’s legislature passed a law authorising the participation of that group in Haiti for another 12 months until October 2027. The law was championed by Bukele and overwhelmingly approved by the country’s congress, controlled by Bukele’s party.
The ongoing clashes with gangs continue as Haiti prepares for its first elections in more than a decade. The country hasn't had a president since Jovenel Moïse was killed in July 2021.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)
Keywords for this article

items.title: French far-left candidate Mélenchon opens door to alliance with rival Greens candidate
items.summary:
French far-left candidate Mélenchon opens door to alliance with rival Greens candidate
French far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon opened the door to an alliance with France's Greens on Thursday after their presidential candidate Marine Tondelier said she was ready to "work on a coalition around" the
items.text:
French far-left candidate Mélenchon opens door to alliance with rival Greens candidate
French far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon opened the door to an alliance with France's Greens on Thursday after their presidential candidate Marine Tondelier said she was ready to "work on a coalition around" the veteran leftist. Tondelier's overture has further boosted Mélenchon's campaign for the Élysée Palace – and angered moderates on the centre-left.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
France's far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon said on Thursday that an alliance with the Greens "should be possible", after Green leader Marine Tondelier triggered criticism from other parties by tentatively agreeing to back him.
Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is leading in the polls to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron next spring, with Mélenchon in second place.
Infighting among centrists and a lack of unity on the left has increased the likelihood of a second-round runoff between Le Pen and Mélenchon.
Read moreFrench presidential election: How far-left Mélenchon became a Gen Z favourite
"We're rather pleased," Mélenchon, the leader of the France Unbowed (LFI) party, told AFP and broadcaster RTL, referring to Tondelier's tentative backing.
"Now we need discussions to take place and for things to move forward. It should be possible to reach a positive outcome," Mélenchon, 75, added.
"It should be doable," he said, while also calling for "cautious restraint".
Speaking during a meeting with supporters, Mélenchon said that discussions were due to begin later on Thursday.
Tondelier, who is polling at around three percent, said on Wednesday evening that Melenchon's campaign momentum was "undeniable".
"So I am saying very clearly that I am ready, and the Greens are ready, to work on a coalition around Jean-Luc Mélenchon's candidacy," Tondelier told France 2 television.
Tondelier's decision must be approved by Green party members in mid-December.
'Capitulation'
Politicians on the centre-left and centre-right criticised her move.
Socialist Party leader Olivier Faure said he regretted her decision, telling broadcaster France 2: "The Greens belong at our side."
Raphaël Glucksmann, the centre-left candidate for the presidential election, was more strident. Tondelier's move risks weakening his bid to rally the left and centre-left around his candidacy.
Recent polls put Glucksmann, the leader of the small Place Publique party, at between 11 percent and 13 percent of voting intentions, while Mélenchon is nearing 20 percent.
Glucksmann attacked both Tondelier and Mélenchon.
"The party that was supposed to be the most pro-federalist party in Europe is going to choose to campaign for a Eurosceptic, for someone who, tweet after tweet, acts as Mr Lavrov's parrot, someone who would abandon the Ukrainian resistance," Glucksmann alleged, referring to Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
Tondelier also earned a strong rebuke from Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, who called her move "a capitulation".
"By taking a back seat to Jean-Luc Mélenchon, Marine Tondelier is putting an end to 50 years of French political ecology that viewed Europe and democracy as its guiding principles," he said on X.
LFI officials, including national coordinator Manuel Bompard, earlier welcomed Tondelier's remarks as "good news" that helps consolidate the party's dominance on the left.
On Thursday, Tondelier toned down her comments.
"I haven't even given my final opinion, which will depend on the discussions," she said, stressing that she remained a candidate herself for now.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
Keywords for this article

items.title: England get one-match suspended ban on away tickets for anti-pope chants in Spain
items.summary:
England have been handed a suspended one-match ban on away ticket sales by Uefa in relation to “racist and/or discriminatory” behaviour by fans at Sunday’s 3-2 Nations League victory over Spain. The punishment is suspended for two years.
Uefa has also fined the Football Association €15,000 (£12,500)
items.text:
England have been handed a suspended one-match ban on away ticket sales by Uefa in relation to “racist and/or discriminatory” behaviour by fans at Sunday’s 3-2 Nations League victory over Spain. The punishment is suspended for two years.
Uefa has also fined the Football Association €15,000 (£12,500), with the behaviour in question believed to be the chant of “Fuck the pope and the IRA” at the Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid. A further charge in the next two years could trigger a ban on away fans for a competitive game.
In a statement given to the Mail, the FA said: “We will not tolerate this unacceptable and deeply offensive chanting, and will work with the police who attend all England home and away matches to identify the perpetrators and take the necessary action.”
Uefa’s control, ethics and disciplinary body announced that it had decided “to fine the English Football Association €15,000 and to order against the English Football Association a full restriction on selling tickets to its supporters for one representative team competition away match, for the racist and/or discriminatory behaviour of its supporters.
“Said full restriction on selling tickets to supporters for one away match is suspended for a probationary period of two years, starting from the date of the present decision.”
The relevant article of Uefa’s disciplinary regulations reads: “If one or more of a member association or club’s supporters engage in the behaviour described in paragraph 1 [insulting the human dignity of a person or group of persons on whatever grounds, including skin colour, race, religion, ethnic origin, gender or sexual orientation], the member association or club responsible incurs a minimum of a fine and either a partial stadium closure or a restriction on selling tickets to its supporters for away matches.”
The match had been preceded by Thomas Tuchel reminding his players of the anti-racism protocols, given the last match between the sides in Madrid, in 2004, had notoriously been marred by abuse aimed at England’s black players.
Last month Spain were fined £15,000 and ordered to play their next friendly with a partial stadium closure after discriminatory chants about Muslims during March’s match against Egypt in Barcelona.
Sunday’s chant is a staple for some England fans but sung relatively rarely in stadiums. Several more frequently heard chants target only the IRA, including inserting “No surrender” into the national anthem.

items.title: OL Lyonnes show their class to hit Arsenal’s ambitions for a top-four WCL finish
items.summary:
Arsenal’s hopes of earning automatic progression to the Champions League quarter-finals were dashed by OL Lyonnes, as the French side continued their statement form in Europe.
Goals in either half from Jule Brand and Melchie Dumornay were the difference at Meadow Park and Lyonnes are top of the tabl
items.text:
Arsenal’s hopes of earning automatic progression to the Champions League quarter-finals were dashed by OL Lyonnes, as the French side continued their statement form in Europe.
Goals in either half from Jule Brand and Melchie Dumornay were the difference at Meadow Park and Lyonnes are top of the table and still yet to concede in the league phase with one game remaining.
It feels like Lyonnes are playing with a fire and intensity fueled by their loss to Barcelona in May’s Champions League final. They look a more formidable, coherent and hungry side, on a mission to end a four-year run without lifting the trophy they won eight times in a 12-year period between 2011 and 2022.
The visit of the eight-time European champions was always going to be challenging for the Gunners and based on current form getting a result would be even tougher. Last season’s runners-up had scored 20 goals without conceding in their first four Champions League matches prior to their trip to Borehamwood and they have scored 49 in their nine Première Ligue games.
The lack of competitiveness in the France top flight also means they were able to rotate heavily at the weekend between their two European games. Jonatan Giráldez made 11 changes for their 1-0 defeat of Saint-Malo on Saturday before returning to his first-choice lineup against the 2025 Champions League winners.
Arsenal were not afforded the luxury of an easy league match after their battling 1-1 draw against Barcelona last week, playing a critical and tricky game with London City Lionesses, which also ended 1-1. Renée Slegers made two changes to the team that hosted ambitious London City, with Ona Batlle having picked up a knock Taylor Hinds played at left-back and Kyra Cooney-Cross started ahead of Kim Little.
They had their backs against the wall at a bitterly cold Meadow Park, as Giráldez’s Galacticos controlled the game. The away team had almost 69% possession in the first half and amassed 12 shots to Arsenal’s one.
The surprise was that Lyonnes weren’t further ahead at the break, with Brand’s 24th-minute goal the difference, the full-back sweeping in Vicki Bècho’s ball in from the right.
Brand was back to haunt the Gunners, having scored in both legs of last season’s semi-final between the two teams, with the French side progressing to face Barcelona in the final with a 4-3 aggregate win.
Arsenal were better after the break, but Lyonnes soaked up a brief spell of Arsenal pressure, Marie-Antoinette Katoto the only player left forward as they banked back and crowded the box to give the home players few options.
They increased their margin and dampened the mood soon after, Tabitha Chawinga’s cross from the left was collected by Katoto and the France forward laid it off for Dumornay who took a touch before powering the ball into the roof of the net.
It was an emphatic and unstoppable finish from one of the best players in the world as a mist lowered over Meadow Park.
It was a testament to the relationship between the club and the fans that the crowd remained in full voice, they urged the players in red and white forward, the North Bank doing all it could to lift the spirits of their struggling side.
There were no more goals and Arsenal’s single shot on target was almost the last kick of the game as a controlled Lyonnes performance demonstrated the gulf in quality between the sides.
Arsenal need to quickly move on, with West Ham their last game before the international break. They had needed a win to have any serious chance of earning a place in top four, avoiding a quarter-final playoff place.
They now sit eighth and will face Inter in their final league phase match in December, with the Italian side needing a win against the north London team to keep any hopes of a playoff place alive. That will not be easy, but a seeded playoff place is in their hands, if they want it.

items.title: A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
items.summary:
“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.
A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
Tracking the stock price amid Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs and alleged spy scandal.
By T
items.text:
“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.
A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
Tracking the stock price amid Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs and alleged spy scandal.
By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.
Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors.
“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”
But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.
The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.
Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.
It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.
On October 29th, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies believed Jensen Huang to be the target of a Chinese espionage plot. The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and one of Nvidia’s clients. Nvidia initially contested the report, adding that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang “are not unusual or unexpected.”
Nvidia’s stock seemingly remained unaffected by the reports, at least at first. The share price closed at $213.66 on October 29th, down just 0.8 percent from the previous day. (Julian Barnes, one of the reporters on the story, later commented, “I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted.”) The stock closed at a 4 percent drop the next day as the entire Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent, the worst single-day decline since June.
The stock continued to fall through Wednesday, November 4th, the day after the blue wave swept the midterms, stoking fears on Wall Street that the new class of Democratic governors in key states like Texas would slow down data center construction. On Thursday, November 5th, Nvidia’s stock fell 9.2 percent, its largest single-day drop in at least a year. But chip stocks began to recover the next day, and by close on Friday, November 6th, Nvidia was back up 2.8 percent to a share price of $186.64.
Then all hell broke loose. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang sent a company-wide memo to Nvidia staff in which he apologized for engaging in an extramarital affair. The memo coincided with the opening of an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into Huang’s alleged misconduct and whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. Huang said he would cooperate fully with the investigation. By the opening bell on Monday, November 9th, Nvidia shares had tumbled 7 percent and trading volume surged past its three-month average as investors reacted to the memo. After a brief rebound, the stock continued to oscillate the next day, as more details of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship emerged. By the time the market closed on Tuesday, November 10th, Nvidia shares were down to $168.89, nearly 10 percent below the closing price on the last day of 2025.
The stock rebounded slightly on Wednesday, November 11th, as investors prepared for Nvidia’s third quarter earnings call, scheduled for the following Tuesday, November 17th. By Wednesday night, however, shares had plunged yet again as media reports circulated that Nvidia’s board was considering ousting Huang, and other reports emerged detailing a second alleged affair, this time between Huang and an Nvidia employee.
Nvidia announced Huang’s departure on the morning of Thursday, November 12th, sending the company’s shares falling nearly 14 percent at the open. It closed at just a 4.3 percent dip. The intraday low of $148.80 per share was its lowest price in a year.
On December 1st, Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews. Nvidia’s general counsel will do the same on December 2nd.
Retail investors have already seized the opportunity to buy the dip. In the first 30 minutes of trading on Thursday, November 12th, retail investors bought $11

items.title: US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months
items.summary:
US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months
The US House Foreign Committee released the chip export licensing data amid Nvidia’s ex-CEO’s affair with alleged Chinese spy.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump approved exports of nearly 900,000 advanc
items.text:
US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months
The US House Foreign Committee released the chip export licensing data amid Nvidia’s ex-CEO’s affair with alleged Chinese spy.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump approved exports of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee has said.
The Department of Commerce’s approvals covered exports of 879,000 chips, including 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD, the committee said on Thursday.
Companies had sought permission to ship 3.4 million of them to China during the period, committee documents show.
The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the Trump administration faces heightened scrutiny following revelations about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which fuelled renewed calls for a tougher stance against Chinese technology threats.
All four of the Chinese companies highlighted in the committee report are on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies.
The committee chair, Brian Mast, has “exercised his authorities under the Export Control Reform Act to publicly reveal export control license application information regarding NVIDIA and AMD’s AI chip licenses for the People’s Republic of China”, the committee said in a statement. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of the chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X.
News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialling up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.
“The fact that over 30 percent of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle.
Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict conditions and limited volumes”. It added that “despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China”.
AMD did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Former US President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China’s military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.
But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.
Nvidia’s stock ended the day down 3.3 percent, while AMD slumped 7.7 percent and the broader Nasdaq and S&P 500 were down 2.2 percent and 1.8 percent, respectively.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statemen
items.text:
Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported.
When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.”
So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality.
Muse Charm, the company’s push into AI hardware, will allow users to carry a physical personification of its software around in their pocket (or potentially wear it around their neck), talking to it, asking it questions, and giving it commands.
It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not. AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience.
Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging. The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250. On the other hand, Amazon’s all-new Bee Frontier wearable AI device — which transcribes conversations and tracks tasks — lists for $75 and is currently on a Black Friday, 30% off sale of $52.49. Even with its $99/year subscription to let it tie into a user’s apps (photos, emails, etc.), it’s still far less expensive than Muse Charm.

items.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
items.summary:
It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.
Apple Pay went down. NASA’s in
items.text:
It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.
Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an attack that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.
The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after cyber hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the Director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.
Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21 striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.
It does seem like more than a coincidence. It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly.
Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice Chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.
The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.
The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.
This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer told TechCrunch, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said.
Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the Senator wrote on X.
AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with.
In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up.
When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.”
Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said.
Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.”
Actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security issues.
And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said.
“There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.”

items.text:
Haiti police say at least 34 suspected gang members killed in raid
Police say the raid targeted the Martissant area, located on a key route out of Port-au-Prince held by gangs since 2021.
At least 34 suspected gang members were killed in a police operation in Martissant, a neighbourhood in Haiti’s capital that has been under gang control for more than five years, Haitian police said.
Haiti’s National Police, which posted footage of armoured vehicles moving through the neighbourhood, said their officers carried out the raid on Thursday with an anti-gang task force that includes personnel from Vectus Global, the private security firm founded by Blackwater founder Erik Prince.
Police reported no other casualties and said none of the roughly 2,500 Salvadoran troops in Haiti took part.
The Martissant neighbourhood is located along a key road that connects Port-au-Prince to Haiti’s western and southern cities, and was used by thousands of people daily before rival gangs began fighting to control the area in 2021.
The subsequent violence forced at least 19,000 people to flee their homes, according to a July 2022 UN report.
Armed groups have since demanded payment for using the road or shot at cars that have tried to pass through, making it difficult to bring goods in and out of the city.
Separately, the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force said it was stepping up operations in Tabarre after months of night patrols and efforts to identify gang positions.
“The objective is clear: not just to displace gangs, but to dismantle their hold on communities, reclaim territory, and prevent their return,” the force said on X.
In the central Artibonite region, the force said their troops had come under fire while clearing barricades and filling in trenches that gangs had dug along National Route 5, north of the town of Gros-Morne.
“During the operation, gang members opened fire on GSF personnel, who responded and forced them to withdraw,” said the update on X.
The raid in Martissant comes as Salvadoran troops have been carrying out joint operations with Haitian police. El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele initially sent troops to search for four Salvadoran aviation technicians who went missing after an October 18 ambush near Port-au-Prince.
What began as a search for the missing men has since grown into a broader offensive against Haiti’s gangs.

items.summary:
Anthropic becomes most valuable AI firm as shares soar in stock market debut
- Published
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the public stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion.
The artificial intelligence
items.text:
Anthropic becomes most valuable AI firm as shares soar in stock market debut
- Published
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the public stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 per share, showing there is plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.5, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day, with shares hitting $97.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet (down 3%) and Amazon (down 3.9%).
The build-out happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate more quickly tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth $1.5 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
On Thursday, the same day Anthropic went public, a bipartisan group of lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

Thursday 19 November 2026 22:05, UK
Arsenal’s hopes of automatic qualification to the Women’s Champions League quarter-finals are hanging by a thread after they were beaten 2-0 at home by a dominant Lyon in foggy conditions.
The French side, who beat Arsenal in the semi-finals last season, got the better of the Gunners again at Meadow Park on Thursday night with goals from Jule Brand and Melchie Dumornay in each half sealing the victory.
Arsenal barely laid a glove on Lyon - who are yet to concede a goal in this season's Champions League - and now sit eighth in the standings, three points adrift of fourth-placed Chelsea, after their first loss in five league phase matches.

Emily Fox registered Arsenal's only shot on target of the game deep in stoppage-time and the home side could easily have conceded a few more had Marie-Antoinette Katoto not spurned two big opportunities.
Arsenal were also indebted to their goalkeeper, Misa, who produced three big saves in the second half to keep out Tabitha Chawinga, Dumornay and Vicki Becho.
Renee Slegers' side, now without a win in three matches in all competitions, are relying on teams above them to drop points in the final round of matches to avoid having to face a play-off match to secure their passage to the quarter-finals.
Meanwhile, Lyon, who currently sit second in the table, have secured a top-four finish with a game to spare after picking up 13 points from five matches.
Slegers: Lyon were better than us
Arsenal Women boss Renee Slegers to ESPN:
"Tough battle. Congratulations to Lyon who were better than us today. They play good football, physically strong in the duels, fast with the ball and without the ball.
"We had a tough time dealing with it in the first half. Second half we controlled the game better without creating clear-cut chances.
"But then you see how clinical Lyon were from their moments."
On her half-time team talk: "It was 1-0, so we were in the game. Like they had, we need moments as well. We are going to get moments and then how we are going to create it."
Analysis: Reality check for Arsenal
Sky Sports News reporter Uma Gurav at Meadow Park:
"The bigger picture here is that Arsenal have played the best two teams in this competition in two consecutive weeks and they've got just one point out of the two games.
"You have to admit the draw was very tough on them to get both Barcelona and Lyon, but it's also a harsh reality check.
"This Arsenal team won the Champions League just 18 months ago. Now, they're not quite up there with the European elites. Can they get back there anytime soon?"
Is it time to question Arsenal boss Slegers?
Ex-Arsenal striker Lianne Sanderson to ESPN:
"I like Renee but there has to come a time [when we question] why is it that all the players look out of form? Apart from Alessia Russo, how many of those players are actually performing?
"There has to come a point where you have to start questioning Renee. As much as I like Renee and everything she's done.
"Not to compare the two, but it feels like Michael Carrick at Man Utd where you feel like someone has taken the team so far but now what?
"We're all waiting for Arsenal to kick on. That tonight disappointed me because it looked flat."

"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fio
items.text:
Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
- Published
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona has died just days after swallowing a knitted hat that slipped into her enclosure.
"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said on Thursday afternoon.
Fiona swallowed the hat about 10 days ago and was asymptomatic at first but then required emergency care.
The vet staff "tried everything they could to help her" but "despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome", the zoo said.
"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."
Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
While she seemed fine at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.
An ultrasound before her death showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine. A zookeeper said surgery was not an option for full-grown hippos and "our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own".
"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said.
Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
Her story inspired an ice cream flavour as well as a character in Cincinnati's ballet.

A United States appeals court has allowed the administration of President Donald Trump to
items.text:
US appeals court lets Trump end TPS deportation protections for Venezuelans
The appeals court’s ruling prevents a lower-court decision from taking effect, which would block Trump from ending the TPS programme.
A United States appeals court has allowed the administration of President Donald Trump to move forward for now with the removal of deportation protections for Venezuelans.
The ruling on Wednesday cancels out a previous order by a lower-court judge that required the government to restore the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) of Venezuelans, which shields recipients against deportation.
The effort to end the TPS protections has proceeded despite humanitarian concerns.
Since taking office for a second term, Trump has sought to carry out what he calls the largest deportation effort in US history. Part of that agenda has been to roll back programmes like TPS.
But in September 2025, US District Judge Edward Chen blocked the expiration of TPS protections for Venezuelans, arguing that deporting those individuals would put them in harm’s way.
He also ruled that the Trump administration had overstepped its authority by seeking to shorten TPS extensions granted under the preceding president, Joe Biden. Such decisions, Chen added, needed to be taken with “careful study and analysis”.
Some 600,000 Venezuelans in the US were protected under TPS programmes.
The Supreme Court paused Chen’s ruling in October 2025. But that pause expired this month, and Chen’s order was set to take effect on Friday.
On Wednesday, the Trump administration filed an emergency request to the Supreme Court to extend the pause before Thursday’s appeals court ruling.
The appeals court’s decision does not nix the ongoing legal challenges to Trump’s efforts to revoke TPS extensions. But it allows the administration to suspend deportation protections while the challenges make their way through court.
The Trump administration has sought to strip large numbers of immigrants of their legal protections in a bid to render them deportable. Other programmes, like humanitarian parole, have also come under the administration’s scrutiny.
TPS allows foreign nationals already in the US to remain while conditions in their home countries are too dangerous or unstable to return to.
Humanitarian parole, meanwhile, allows people outside the US to come in on a temporary basis, often to escape similarly perilous conditions.
The Trump administration has argued that TPS designations are meant to be temporary — and that previous presidencies extended such protections without cause.
It has also maintained that conditions have improved in places like Venezuela, where a US military action on January 3 resulted in the abduction of President Nicolas Maduro.
Human rights advocates, however, have noted that Maduro’s government remains largely intact. That leadership has been accused of abuses ranging from arbitrary imprisonment to the torture of political dissidents.
The US Department of State currently warns against travel to Venezuela, citing issues such as crime, kidnapping and poor health infrastructure.

items.summary:
Why are Bukele’s Salvadoran troops in Haiti and what have they achieved?
With crowds rallying behind El Salvador’s deployment in Haiti, analysts question whether civilians are any safer.
The streets of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, rang out on Tuesday and Wednesday with chants from local resident
items.text:
Why are Bukele’s Salvadoran troops in Haiti and what have they achieved?
With crowds rallying behind El Salvador’s deployment in Haiti, analysts question whether civilians are any safer.
The streets of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, rang out on Tuesday and Wednesday with chants from local residents in support of a president who was not their own: El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. In a country where the scars of foreign intervention run deep, some Haitians are placing their hopes on another foreign force, this time from El Salvador, to help take their neighbourhoods back from armed gangs.
Thousands turned out to cheer on the roughly 2,500 soldiers Bukele has sent since October. What began as a narrow mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran aviation technicians has grown into a much broader military operation.
For some of those who marched, the intervention is exactly what the country needs after years of kidnappings, killings, and displacement, with little sign of relief.
But even with the Haitian government’s backing and a warm reception from the public, questions are growing about what the troops are doing on the ground and what kind of mark Bukele will ultimately leave on Haiti.
Why are Salvadoran troops in Haiti?
The immediate trigger came on October 18, when four Salvadoran aviation technicians working with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) went missing after armed men attacked their vehicle near Port-au-Prince.
The force was created to help Haitian authorities deal with a security crisis that has grown more severe since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise. According to Reuters, gangs now control more than 80 percent of the capital region, with Haitian and international forces struggling to reclaim that territory.
Shortly after the technicians went missing, Bukele announced a new military operation in Haiti, sending 100 special forces soldiers to rescue them. Since then, he’s sent about 2,500 in total.
Most of them are operating outside the UN-backed force and outside the UN support office’s monitoring mechanisms, according to UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric.
And the deployment itself has turned from a narrow rescue operation to a broader offensive against Haiti’s gangs, with Salvadoran soldiers joining Haitian security forces, the GSF, and private contractors, including Blackwater founder Erik Prince’s Vectus Global.
Bukele, who gained international notoriety for a crackdown on gangs in El Salvador that led to a sharp decline in crime but has drawn widespread condemnation over human rights abuses, has been aggressively promoting the deployment on social media.
He has posted dramatic videos of helicopter attacks on gang leaders’ properties and, more recently, footage of rallies cheering on his troops.
“I never expected anything like this,” he wrote in a Tuesday post accompanying a video of a rally. “I hear you loud and clear. I love you, too.”
Neither the Haitian government nor the Salvadoran government replied to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment about the troops in Haiti.
Why are some Haitians cheering on the Salvadoran troops?
The troops have landed amid a worsening humanitarian crisis in Haiti, with nearly 1.5 million people displaced from their homes, and violence making it difficult to access food and basic services. More than 22,000 people have been killed in gang-related violence, including security operations, since 2022, according to Reuters.
At rallies in Port-au-Prince and other parts of Haiti, demonstrators voiced support for the deployment. Some who spoke to The Associated Press news agency described losing loved ones to gang violence and being forced to leave their homes.
“The support we see from many Haitians comes from sheer desperation after years of failure and widespread terror,” Louimann Maceus, president of the human rights organisation Ensemble des Citoyens Competents a la Recherche de l’Egalite des Droits de l’Homme en Haiti (ECCREDHH), told Al Jazeera. “People are exhausted.”
“There is a genuine hope, especially among the hundreds of thousands of internally displaced people we work with who just want to return safely home,” said Maceus, who lives in Port-au-Prince.
That hope, he said, follows years of frustration with UN-backed forces, which he said had done little to improve security.
The Salvadoran deployment already outnumbers the GSF, according to numbers from the GSF’s special representative Jack Christofides, on October 18, when it had just surpassed 2,000 personnel.
International Crisis Group analyst Diego Da Rin also links some of the enthusiasm to what he describes as a really effective communication campaign by Bukele, whose videos of strikes on gang leaders’ homes are all over Haitian social media.
“These are symbolic wins that everybody was waiting for,” he said, adding that AI-generated videos were also circulating of gang leaders being arrested.
But support for the deployment is not universal. Da Rin pointed to the residents of gang-controlled areas.
“Many of these people, who clearly see the risks in these iron-fist operations, are extremely scared of being attacked and being collateral damage of any of these operations,” said Da Rin.
What have Salvadoran troops actually achieved?
Security force clashes and drone strikes targeting gangs increased by 46 percent in the 21 days after the start of the deployment, compared to the 21 days before it, according to the conflict monitoring group the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED).
ACLED estimated more than 100 people were killed in the same period, including at least 26 civilians.
Haiti’s Justice Minister Patrick Pelissier, however, said on Monday that the government had received no reports of civilian casualties in the latest operations, which it described as professional, according to Reuters.
Bukele has used social media to highlight what he sees as the offensive’s successes.
