items.title: Fuck Your AI Safeguards
items.summary:
Fuck your AI safeguards
While refrigerators were getting hacked in Estonia, I half-seriously took a project I’m working on and asked Claude Code if there are any low-hanging fruit regarding security that we could improve. It found one issue that was easy to fix, simple oversight with a one line fix,
items.text:
Fuck your AI safeguards
While refrigerators were getting hacked in Estonia, I half-seriously took a project I’m working on and asked Claude Code if there are any low-hanging fruit regarding security that we could improve. It found one issue that was easy to fix, simple oversight with a one line fix, so I just went along with it.
Then it got stopped because of bullshit “AI safeguards”. Oh no, how dare I, the senior product engineer with my product that I provably have control over, try to fix and prevent security issues and ensure compliance with local laws and regulations?
“Oh but you can just apply to get an exemption from them here bla bla fucking blah”
Have you READ the requirements?
First of all, you will have to wait for multiple business days to get a response.
You forfeit any data retention exemptions, so hope you don’t have any IP to protect!
Oh, and oh so please give us your fucking ID or passport! We won’t leak it later, promise!
And you may just get fucked anyway and not get approval. Approval to appropriately protect your own service!
This wasn’t the first time I ran into this issue. As maddening as it sounds, I try to keep up with the security landscape and to apply appropriate mitigations because leaking sensitive information is a big fucking no-no and I can’t let that happen.
If there’s a popular exploit out there that applies for our technical stack, I need to know if the public proof-of-concept snippets can be adapted and used maliciously against my services. But no, Claude will tell you to fuck off and use an older model that still will try to stop you from applying adequate protection.
You know who don’t need to ask for approval? Criminals. They just go and use the models that don’t have safeguards in place. Abliterated open weights models don’t care. Bad actors reach their goals with or without your “safe” models.
You can use a knife to cut up some food, or seriously hurt someone. Yet I don’t get asked to put in an application with my government-provided ID to buy one. Why is this tool so special?
Predictably, the only way to actually make our own service more secure ended up involving the use of EU-hosted open weights models, such as GLM 5.3, that actually complied with our intentions, proved that the issue is there, and then helped fix and verify that the issue is now resolved, for good.
Congratulations, Anthropic, you’ve made the world an unsafer place.
Or maybe that was your plan all along to get regulators to react and build that moat for you right before your IPO to fend off competitors?
Either way, I’m just incredibly frustrated. Big AI labs use the same tools without restrictions to make the security landscape a fucking mess, and then they go and prohibit others from using the same tools to protect themselves from the threats they just created. Fucking asshats.1
- and that’s my swear word quota hit for the year. ↩︎

Bellarena will be TGR Design’s first course in Northern Ireland and the first new championship links to open in Northern Ireland in more than a century; TGR Design are a golf course design firm led by Tiger Woods
Thursday 19 November 2026 16:41, UK
Tiger Woods has revealed he will design the first championship-standard links golf course built in Northern Ireland for more than 100 years, describing the project as a "special opportunity".
Reports linking the 15-time major champion with the proposed £30 million course at Bellarena on the north west coast between Limavady and Coleraine had been circulating for several weeks, ahead of Thursday's official announcement.
Hospitality group Galgorm Collection is building the course, with construction set to get under way next year if the required planning approvals are secured.

In a statement, Woods said: "Northern Ireland is home to some of the greatest links golf in the world, and building one on the Causeway Coast is a special opportunity for our team.
"We want Bellarena to feel as though it has always been part of this coastline, with a course that challenges the best players and is fun for everyone who plays it."
Galgorm Collection already owns and runs the championship parkland course at Galgorm Castle in Ballymena and a course at Roe Valley in Limavady, with plans to create an additional venue
Colin Johnston, chief executive of Galgorm Collection, announced that Woods and his TGR Design firm would craft the new links layout.
"Set against the spectacular backdrop of Northern Ireland's rugged northwest coast, our plans represent a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform Northern Ireland's golfing and tourism future," Johnston said.
Bellarena is around 20 miles from Royal Portrush Golf Club, which hosted Shane Lowry's win at The Open in 2019 and Scottie Scheffler completing the third leg of the career Grand Slam in 2025.
Portstewart - host of Jon Rahm's win at the 2017 Irish Open - and Castlerock also boast acclaimed links courses in the region.
Reef Destinations has previously worked with TGR Design on course construction projects in the United States. Bellarena already has a historical link with the United States as a site of a US Army base during the Second World War.
When will Woods next feature?
Woods is poised to return to competitive golf next month for the first time in over two years after being confirmed as an entrant at the Hero World Challenge in the Bahamas from December 3-6.
The 50-year-old has not played competitively since The Open at Royal Troon in 2024 and has played limited golf since a career-threatening car crash in Florida in 2021.
Woods has had at least three different surgeries since his last start and spent time at a rehab facility in Switzerland earlier this year, having been arrested and charged with driving under the influence following a car crash near his home.

items.title: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order
items.summary:
UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order
The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has rejected the UK government’s attempt to keep its order secret, marking a significant victory for transparency.
There's something pretty extraordinary about a government being able to demand
items.text:
UK Government Forced to Admit It Issued Apple a Secret Encryption Order
The Investigatory Powers Tribunal has rejected the UK government’s attempt to keep its order secret, marking a significant victory for transparency.
There's something pretty extraordinary about a government being able to demand changes to the security of devices used by millions of people, prevent a company that makes those devices from discussing those demands, and then refuse to even acknowledge that the demands exist at all.
That has been the sordid situation surrounding the UK governement's ongoing dispute with Apple over encrypted iCloud data. Up until today, the UK government's position has essentially been that it would neither confirm nor deny whether it issued Apple with a Technical Capability Notice (TCN). These are secret orders issued under Section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which gives the UK government powers to require technology companies to make changes to their services to facilitate the exercise of investigatory powers. Today, the Investigatory Powers Tribunal has ruled that the UK government must acknowledge that it issued Apple with such a notice.
This is a big deal. Whilst it doesn't mean we suddenly know everything the UK government wants Apple to do, the government's attempt to keep even the existence of the order secret has now suffered a major defeat.
I covered the background to this extensively in my piece, Two-Tier Encryption in the UK. The story goes back to February 2025 when the Washington Post exposed that the government had ordered Apple to provide ‘backdoor’ access to encrypted iCloud data, belonging not just to users in the UK, but around the world. The order was reportedly issued in January 2025 under the Investigatory Powers Act — the centrepiece of the UK’s modern surveillance law.
Rather than weaken its security provisions, Apple took the quite extraordinary step of withdrawing Advanced Data Protection (ADP) from new UK users. ADP is an optional feature that extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data — when enabled, even Apple can't decrypt the protected information.[1] Apple subsequently made clear that it would not build a backdoor or a master key into any of its products or services. They stated this without publicly referencing the Technical Capability Notice, as they were forbidden from doing so.
The original order's scope extended beyond British users — it potentially implicated the encrypted data of Apple's customers all around the world, including the United States. Following months of diplomatic wrangling involving the Trump administration, the UK government withdrew that original notice, but that wasn't the end of it. The UK government issued a second Technical Capability Notice, this time reportedly restricted to British users. Apple's original legal challenge was subsequently dismissed following with the withdrawal of the first notice, so the company launched a fresh legal challenge in 2026.
The difficulty for the UK government has always been that the existence of the original order was already widely reported. The Washington Post had published its exposé, and many other news outlets subsequently reported on it. The UK government nevertheless maintained its position of neither confirming nor denying the existence of individual TCNs.
At a hearing at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on 17 September this year, lawyers representing civil rights organisations Liberty and Privacy International challenged that position. Ben Jaffey KC, representing the organisations, argued that the UK government's insistence on maintaining secrecy had become increasingly difficult to justify. Jaffey compared the secrecy order to the “emperor’s new clothes… and brings the administration of justice into disrepute”.
The existence of the order was already public knowledge and continuing to pretend otherwise was obstructing the proper consideration of the legal challenge. The UK government disagreed, arguing that abandoning its neither-confirm-nor-deny policy could damage national security by assisting hostile actors in building a picture of which companies were subject to such notices. Today the tribunal rejected that argument.
As Reuters reports, the Tribunal concluded:
“The respondent has not established that it would be damaging to national security to reveal in these proceedings, as is the case, that the respondent has given Apple a Technical Capability Notice.”
The Tribunal hasn't ruled that the underlying order was unlawful; it hasn't made a determination whether the UK government can legitimately require Apple to make changes to its encryption systems; it hasn't disclosed the precise technical requirements of the notice. But the government has lost an important argument about keeping the proceedings secret.
In my Two-Tier Encryption in the UK piece, I used the idea of “Alice and Bill”, two fictional people living in the UK, both using identical iPhones and both paying for iCloud, to illustrate a fundamental problem that had arisen from the dispute between Apple and the UK government.
Alice had enabled Advanced Data Protection before Apple withdrew the feature for new UK users, Bill hadn't. Alice continued to benefit from Apple's strongest available iCloud encryption protections, Bill couldn't even enable them. The result was a peculiar situation in which two customers using the same service had materially different levels of protection.
Because Apple withdrew ADP for new UK users in February 2025, existing users who had already enabled the feature have not since been required to turn it off — Apple’s security documentation says its servers can’t modify the ADP setting, or roll it back on a user’s behalf. This has created a ‘two-tier’ system of protection based on when somebody enabled a particular security feature.

items.summary:

IEBC Com
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has apologised to political party leaders following a chaotic consultative meeting in Nairobi, pledging to tighten security and enforce stricter admission protocols to prevent a recurrence of the disruptions.
IEBC Commissioner Alutalala Mukhwana offered the apology on behalf of the commission after United Democratic Alliance (UDA) chairperson Cecily Mbarire protested what she described as harassment and intimidation of party officials by individuals she claimed were not authorised to attend the meeting.
Mukhwana acknowledged that there had been commotion at the venue before the meeting commenced, admitting that the commission had not anticipated the presence of unauthorised individuals and the treatment allegedly meted out to some delegates.
” We did not know that there would be infiltration and this kind of treatment that is being committed on our officials. This is unacceptable, there can be no excuse and we are deeply sorry,” he said.
He assured political leaders that the commission had taken note of the complaints and would strengthen security arrangements to ensure that only invited participants gain access to future consultative meetings.
The commissioner said the commission’s security team, led by its head of security, Natasha, would be mobilised to enforce tighter controls at subsequent engagements.
“We will mobilise enough and we will make sure that only those who are getting invited will be admitted to the venue,” he said.
The apology followed a heated protest by Mbarire, who threatened to withdraw UDA from future IEBC meetings unless the commission guaranteed order, security and equal treatment of all political parties.
The Embu Governor accused individuals she described as unknown bodyguards attached to opposition leaders of interfering with seating arrangements and harassing UDA officials.
“We will not attend any more of your meetings. You tell me why we need people from outside. They are not even known bodyguards. They come here to harass us and take away seats from some of us. That’s not fair,” Mbarire said.
She challenged IEBC chairperson Erastus Ethekon to take responsibility for the commission’s engagements, questioning how the electoral body could guarantee a free and fair election if it could not maintain order during a stakeholder meeting.
“If you cannot take charge of your own meeting and ensure that the people who enter in the room while you are holding the meeting are people who ought to come, then you tell me how you run a general election,” she said.
Mbarire demanded that the commission use uniformed police officers for security instead of individuals she accused of intimidating delegates.
“If you need security, bring police officers in uniform. Not some guys here who are, you know, literally harassing everybody else,” she added.
She insisted that all political party leaders were equal stakeholders and should be accorded equal treatment during the consultations.
Mukhwana acknowledged the complaints, saying the commission regretted the incident and would take measures to ensure that future meetings were properly managed.
The commissioner further assured Mbarire that the commission would take responsibility for managing its meetings, acknowledging that political consultations required proper coordination and respect for all participants.
The incident also drew protests from Kisii Governor Simba Arati, who backed Mbarire’s concerns and called on the commission to enforce discipline among political leaders and their representatives.
Arati warned that political parties would not tolerate disorder during engagements with the electoral body, saying cooperation must be accompanied by mutual respect.
The disruption came against the backdrop of a separate confrontation between IEBC and opposition leaders, who staged a walkout after rejecting the agenda presented by the commission.
Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i and former Chief Justice David Maraga were among those who withdrew from the meeting.
The opposition accused IEBC of failing to incorporate key electoral concerns into its agenda, arguing that the commission had not adequately consulted them despite repeated requests for engagement.
Gachagua said correspondence sent to the commission, including letters dated May 10 and June 24, 2026, seeking the establishment of a technical team to discuss electoral reforms, had gone unanswered.
The opposition proposed that a team led by Maraga engage the commission to develop a comprehensive agenda incorporating issues they consider critical to the credibility of the August 2027 General Election.
Among their demands are a clean and verifiable voter register, abolition of the national presidential tallying centre at Bomas of Kenya, electronic voting for Kenyans in the diaspora and livestreaming of voting, counting and announcement of results at polling stations and tallying centres.
Kalonzo subsequently said the opposition had attended the engagement in good faith but was dissatisfied with what he described as the commission’s failure to demonstrate independence, impartiality and preparedness.
The two confrontations exposed the competing demands facing IEBC as it seeks to build consensus among political parties ahead of the next General Election.
While the opposition wants substantive electoral reforms incorporated into the commission’s consultations, UDA is demanding tighter control of meeting access, security arrangements and equal treatment of political party representatives.
IEBC has indicated that it will continue engaging political parties and other stakeholders as part of preparations for the 2027 elections, with Ethekon announcing that broader consultations would begin the following week.

items.summary: As Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday in the largest IPO in history, CEO Dario Amodei reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing AI responsibly. In his speech ahead of the Nasdaq opening bell, Amodei vowed that the AI company would not bend to either business or political pressu
items.text:
As Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday in the largest IPO in history, CEO Dario Amodei reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing AI responsibly. In his speech ahead of the Nasdaq opening bell, Amodei vowed that the AI company would not bend to either business or political pressure and would “remain under human control.”
Reading the speech from a printout, the CEO began by talking about Anthropic’s origins as a way to build powerful technology to help humanity — something that he said was inspired by the loss of his father to a disease that became curable just a few years later.
He acknowledged that while human intelligence had made diseases like the plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world, there were still too few scientists with too little time to make progress in other areas of disease. AI, he said, could help with this by working in concert with humans to further medical progress.
It’s telling that Amodei began with a story highlighting AI’s potentially life-saving applications, since he’s warned repeatedly about the risks of advancing the technology too quickly. In September, Amodei drew headlines when he outlined a plan to pace AI development, which included things like coordinating with other leading companies on safety standards and embedding evaluators from third-party organizations to verify that companies were following their safety commitments.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, and xAI owner Elon Musk said they agreed with Amodei’s position, although few concrete commitments have been made.
In this morning’s speech, Amodei again stressed the need to progress AI technology and the safety required in doing so. He referred to the “very real risks” of AI in the hands of bad actors, whether those were individuals or nation-states, and the potential for things like “economic disruption” and “losing control of AI systems.”
Anthropic believes these risks are avoidable, he noted, as long as there are safeguards in place. Amodei said the company would continue to be invested in the work of AI alignment and testing, and developing new ways to understand AI behavior so it could remain under human control.
“There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us,” he said. “The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed more so than it has already towards double and triple checking that those AI systems are safe and remain under human control.”
“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei concluded.
His sister, Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, echoed these sentiments in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, noting that while the risks were real, the promise of AI was also “incredible.”
“We were really founded on this idea that it is our job to mitigate those risks, and I think we have to date done an incredible job doing that. We obviously have more work ahead of us, but we are deeply committed to safety,” she added. 
The full text of Dario Amodei’s opening speech is below:
Thank you, Daniela. My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind. Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that just a few years later became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments. So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket — tools for gene editing, tools for gene synthesis, tools for controlling brain cells with light — started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking, from intelligence.
Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades. It took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR. Nature is full of these patterns, but we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them. Too few scientists with too [little] time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would have taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.
I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point, all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time, and although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe these processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by a few years. Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many other applications of Claude. Our customers, the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people, are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth, lift people out of poverty, protect democracy and free societies, even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them, and I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

items.text:
Struggling Blackpool sack Evatt on his birthday
- Published
Blackpool have sacked head coach Ian Evatt on his 45th birthday after a year in charge following a run of one win and six defeats in their past 10 league games.
Evatt's final match was Saturday's 1-0 away defeat by fellow strugglers AFC Wimbledon, leaving the Tangerines immediately above the League One relegation zone.
That defeat, however, came after the he said his squad had been decimated by a sickness bug during their trip to the capital.
Evatt departs the Seasiders with the announcement made a matter of hours after the club wished him a happy birthday, external on social media.
In a statement, the club thanked Evatt for his efforts and said Steve Thompson will take charge for Saturday's game against Wigan Athletic.
Blackpool appointed Evatt, who won promotion from League One and the Championship during seven years as a centre-back for the club, as Steve Bruce's successor in October 2025.
During a six-year playing career at Bloomfield Road, Evatt made more than 250 appearances for the Seasiders.
On arrival as a manager, a tally of 13 points from a possible 15 in December 2025 lifted them out of the relegation zone, although they lost 10 and won two of their next 15 matches in all competitions.
They finished the campaign strongly, with six wins in seven games as part of a sequence of one defeat in 13 between mid-March and the end of August, only to struggle again as this season continued.
Speaking after their defeat by Mansfield in October, Evatt said he had "a huge amount of confidence" in his ability because of his record.
Evatt guided Barrow to the 2019-20 National League title in his first managerial role, then won promotion to League One with Bolton Wanderers the following season.
Wanderers went on to lift the 2022-23 EFL Trophy and reached the third-tier play-offs in consecutive seasons under Evatt, losing in the final in his final full campaign in 2023-24.
- 'It's been horrific' - Evatt says sickness bug decimated Blackpool 
  - Published3 days ago
Evatt will retain legendary status despite exit - analysis
BBC Radio Lancashire sport editor Andy Bayes
After an encouraging start to the season, Blackpool's form has been alarming since the beginning of September, and owner-chairman Simon Sadler has decided a change was needed with 33 league matches still to play.
There have been mitigating circumstances but everyone in the hot seat is judged on their points return.
His final game in charge will undoubtedly go down as one of those factors. Illness within the squad made the defeat at Wimbledon somewhat understandable, but the performance should have warranted more.
Throughout Evatt's tenure, he was forced to constantly juggle an injury list that never seemed to ease.
The centre-back position was a recurring problem and is unlikely to be solved overnight. Steve Bruce signings Fraser Horsfall and Michael Ihiekwe have yet to make a league appearance this season, despite being expected to play a significant role after injuries at the back end of the last campaign.
Supporters wanted greater tactical flexibility and a system that would allow mercurial talents such as Josh Bowler to have a greater impact.
However, Evatt largely stuck with a wing-back formation, believing he did not have the personnel to play effectively in other ways.
He made an immediate impact after taking charge, but that was followed by a significant downturn in form before a recovery that secured League One survival last season.
This term, there had been hope that those struggles were behind Blackpool.
Evatt will retain legendary status for his achievements as a player, having won two promotions and played in the Premier League.
However, Blackpool are now searching for their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Sadler took over the club in the summer of 2019.

items.title: Premier League clubs vote to increase legal protection for executives
items.summary:
Clubs rallied behind the Premier League’s leadership in a key vote on Thursday, overwhelmingly backing new rules that would protect the chief executive, Richard Masters, from potentially damaging lawsuits.
A vote to expand the legal indemnity afforded to Premier League directors was won 18-2 at a sh
items.text:
Clubs rallied behind the Premier League’s leadership in a key vote on Thursday, overwhelmingly backing new rules that would protect the chief executive, Richard Masters, from potentially damaging lawsuits.
A vote to expand the legal indemnity afforded to Premier League directors was won 18-2 at a shareholders’ meeting in central London, granting Masters and other figures greater protection in the event they were subjected to legal action as a consequence of doing their job.
Manchester City are understood to be one of two clubs to vote against the extension of indemnity, and one unnamed side spoke out at length against the measures during the meeting. The other vote against was by Nottingham Forest, who felt insufficient time had been granted to consider the proposal. The rule change follows reports that the organisation’s leadership may be named in possible legal action by City’s Abu Dhabi sponsors, who have claimed their reputations were damaged as a result of the excoriating verdict of an independent commission regarding City’s breaches of the league’s financial rules. City have appealed against the verdict.
This week the Abu Dhabi telecommunications giant and City sponsor Etisalat released a statement describing the contents of the verdict as “entirely false and defamatory”. Referring to the independent commission’s report as “the published findings of the English Premier League”, Etisalat said it was “actively considering all options relating to its rights and associated legal remedies in this matter”.
The details of any increase of indemnity, including who would cover any potential costs, were not discussed in the meeting.
The chief refereeing officer of Pro Ref, Howard Webb, attended and came under sustained questioning from club executives over recent referee and video assistant referee failures.
A report by the independent key match incidents panel this week found there had been two serious mistakes that were not corrected by the VAR during the most recent round of matches. Webb is understood to have acknowledged that performance in matchday 10 had been “poor” but argued that apart from that weekend, key metrics on decision-making had been trending in the right direction this season.
The Premier League has confirmed next season will begin on Friday, 13 August and finish on 21 May. It said players would have 75 “clear days” break at the end of the current season.

items.title: Fifa sparks tension with demand for tax-free status in UK for Women’s World Cup
items.summary:
Fifa is at loggerheads with the UK’s government and four Football Associations over the world governing body’s demands for tax-free status and exemptions from exchange-rate fees at the 2035 Women’s World Cup.
The UK bid to host the tournament is due to be ratified at an extraordinary Fifa congress i
items.text:
Fifa is at loggerheads with the UK’s government and four Football Associations over the world governing body’s demands for tax-free status and exemptions from exchange-rate fees at the 2035 Women’s World Cup.
The UK bid to host the tournament is due to be ratified at an extraordinary Fifa congress in Zurich on Monday, and the Guardian has learned there is tension behind the scenes over many of Fifa’s requirements, which multiple sources involved in the discussions have indicated will not be met.
Fifa is understood to have requested blanket exemptions on tax for all football-related activities for it and its broadcast and commercial partners, as well as its suppliers and staff.
It also wants ticket sales, which have been projected to reach 4.5m for the 48-team competition, to be VAT-free and for currency exchange fees to be waived.
Government sources have told the Guardian such blanket exemptions will not be granted, for financial reasons and the optics of giving tax breaks to Fifa, which has cash reserves of more than $4bn (£3bn).
Fifa’s governance crisis has also complicated matters, with Andy Burnham having called on Gianni Infantino to resign on multiple occasions, and the FA preparing to endorse Philippe Diallo at March’s presidential election.
Negotiations involving Fifa, the Treasury and the domestic FAs will continue after the UK bid has been ratified. Some carveouts may be granted but the government is adamant the World Cup will not receive the wholesale tax-free status Fifa is seeking.
“We provided every guarantee that we can provide under the laws of the country and flagged any deviations transparently,” an FA spokesperson said. “Our approach is also consistent with every major event the UK has hosted or is due to host, including London 2012 and Euro 2028.”
Fifa identified in its evaluation report of the UK bid the UK’s tax and legal framework as a “medium risk” for the tournament, which would need to be addressed.
Fifa’s tax requirements have proved challenging for many tournament hosts in recent years, including in relation to last summer’s men’s World Cup. After months of negotiations with the US treasury, Fifa succeeded in securing a late exemption from federal taxes for the 48 competing teams, although many were forced to pay state and city tax on their World Cup earnings depending on the location of their matches.
The tax adviser Oriana Morrison, who has worked for many national associations, said: “Fifa will ask for the world but ultimately accept the minimum that enables the tournament to be commercially viable. There are likely to be some difficult conversations ahead as the tournament will not generate anywhere near as much money as the men’s World Cup, so the margins are far tighter.”
Fifa has been approached for comment.

items.text:
WBC open door for Canelo Alvarez to challenge Britain's Willy Hutchinson for light-heavyweight world championship
The WBC did not put in place a mandatory challenger for new light-heavyweight world champion Willy Hutchinson; that leaves the path open for Mexican superstar Canelo Alvarez to return to 175lbs and take on Hutchinson; Canelo returned from Terence Crawford defeat to reclaim WBC 168lbs title
Thursday 19 November 2026 13:18, UK
The door is open for Canelo Alvarez to move back to light-heavyweight and challenge new world champion Willy Hutchinson.
Scotland's Hutchinson won his rematch with Joshua Buatsi on November 7 to secure the vacant WBC light-heavyweight title.
Mexican superstar Alvarez reclaimed the WBC's super-middleweight belt when he outscored Christian Mbilli at the end of last month.
Although 168lbs is his natural weight, Canelo has previous boxed at light-heavyweight, beating Sergey Kovalev but losing to Dmitry Bivol.
The WBC would approve Hutchinson making a first title defence against Canelo.
"Yes, absolutely," WBC president Mauricio Sulaiman told Sky Sports.
"Canelo's win is very fresh after a year of huge difficulties, dealing with a loss against [Terence] Crawford, dealing with an injury and a surgery, then having to come back.
"The way he conquered the title and he celebrated, he's taken some time off."
WBC haven't ordered a mandatory challenger yet for the Briton, leaving that path to Hutchinson open for Alvarez.
"We will see what happens in the following days. At the convention we left that division open without a ruling. We're going to wait and not anticipate and we will see what happens in the following weeks and Canelo Alvarez certainly is a possibility [for Hutchinson]," Sulaiman said.
"If he decides to challenge at light-heavyweight, it would certainly be approved, champion against champion, if he decides to stay at super-middleweight there are certain alternatives."
The WBC president added: "I'm very proud of Hutchinson. He proved us right, there were many complaints about him fighting for the title but he proved us right and he won and he's deservedly the WBC champion."

items.title: Football Daily | Football’s political gamers face off at Fifa with the real-life final boss
items.summary:
GAME ON!
Although the millions of gamers who are pulling sickies would beg to differ, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI wasn’t the most exciting midnight launch involving a sprawling enterprise full of shady characters. Over in Zurich, the clock also struck 12 on the candidate deadline for next yea
items.text:
GAME ON!
Although the millions of gamers who are pulling sickies would beg to differ, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI wasn’t the most exciting midnight launch involving a sprawling enterprise full of shady characters. Over in Zurich, the clock also struck 12 on the candidate deadline for next year’s Fifa presidential election, leaving those of us who have no interest in video games with our own chaotic, multi-billion-dollar sandbox where untouchable bosses bend the rules to suit themselves. While online carjackers are busy exploring a “most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world”, football’s real-life power brokers are gearing up for a March showdown in the actual city of Rabat.
For years, Gianni Infantino has looked nailed-on to glide into a fourth term of office completely unopposed, but following his disastrous Fifa Forward Enterprise wheeze to flog stakes in the World Cup to his American pals on the cheap, many of the emperor’s former allies have finally turned against him. In the wake of the revolt, European national associations withdrew their backing for Infantino and, on Thursday morning, Fifa confirmed the 56-year-old will face his first contested election since parking his backside on the throne a decade ago. Sadly for all those who would like nothing more than to see him deposed, Infantino remains the red-hot favourite in what will be a three-horse race.
Leading the charge for the mutineers is Philippe Diallo, the 63-year-old French Football Federation president who was unanimously anointed as Europe’s preferred candidate after their actual preferred candidate, Arsène Wenger, decided not to throw his chapeau in the ring. His billing by Uefa’s vice-president, Laura McAllister, as a man “who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform” at Fifa conveniently overlooks the fact that, as recently as five months ago, Diallo’s own federation signed a letter formally endorsing Infantino again. Joining Diallo in the battle to prise Gianni’s fingers off the levers of power is Kozo Tashima, the 68-year-old honorary president of the Japan FA. He could yet stand aside to avoid a split of the vote from Fifa’s 211 members who want Infantino booted to the door marked “Do One!”. Unfortunately, Ramon Vega, the former Switzerland and Tottenham defender, won’t be on the ballot. He had again announced his candidacy but proved unable to scare up the five member-association endorsements required.
Between now and Fifa’s March congress, all three candidates must pass a Fifa eligibility and integrity check, a feat which shouldn’t be beyond the two pretenders, given Infantino has repeatedly come through it with flying colours while helping to overhaul the committees tasked with marking his papers along the way. Assuming he once again clears the hurdle of being vetted by his own organisation, the next four months promise a familiar blur of private jets, palm-greasing and disingenuous crawling. While a generation of gamers will spend winter pulling off virtual heists in Vice City, when it comes to bending the rules in your favour, nobody plays the game quite like the Fifa final boss.
LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE
Join Yara El-Shaboury from 8pm GMT for minute-by-minute updates from Arsenal 1-1 OL Lyonnes in Women’s Bigger Cup.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“It’s not that I don’t ‘care’ about the price, it’s that the market is the market; it doesn’t depend on me. Calmness always, perspective … I know strikers are measured by goals but, well, the days I don’t score I’m sure I will be able to walk off the pitch and say that, no matter what happened, I helped my team, doing a load of other things. It is what it is” – Gonzalo García, the Spanish U-21 forward and great nephew of Rita Hayworth, gets his chat on with Sid Lowe about his £34m switch to Fulham, the pace of the Premier League and more.
RECOMMENDED SUBSCRIBING
Sport in Focus picks out the best photos of the past seven days. Get it delivered to your inbox every Friday by signing up here.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 When I first saw the photo in yesterday’s Football Daily, I thought Mauricio Pochettino had opted for a short back and sides, presumably to pre-empt him tearing his luscious locks out in frustration at forthcoming poor results/terrible January transfer window/petulant sniping from sulky squad members. Then I realised he was in the back seat, all but entirely obscured by the rear-view mirror, in which he could perhaps see his sense of job satisfaction disappearing …” – Phil Taverner.
 That photo of Pochettino being chauffeured by a beefy driver answered one of my burning questions: what’s Ange Postecoglou doing these days?” – Mike Wilner (and others).
If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Phil Taverner. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

It’s rolling out now globally on all ChatGPT plans on the web, desktop app, and iOS and Android apps. While using dictation i
items.text:
ChatGPT can receive audio prompts from your microphone faster now with a Live Dictation feature that transcribes as you speak, rather than waiting until you finish recording. It’s rolling out now globally on all ChatGPT plans on the web, desktop app, and iOS and Android apps. While using dictation in ChatGPT, you can tap or click the audio waveform to show the live text transcript the AI is generating, then edit it in the prompt box when you’re done.
ChatGPT can transcribe as you speak now with Live Dictation
ChatGPT’s new Live Dictation feature transcribes audio prompts faster, with no more 10-minute limit.
Along with faster transcription, OpenAI also announced it’s removing the 10-minute recording limit on voice dictation in ChatGPT, and it says the feature is getting “more reliable.” The update follows an overhaul for ChatGPT’s two-way conversational voice mode earlier this year. Last year, OpenAI also announced a “record mode” for transcribing voice notes and meetings. That feature is still in beta and limited to Plus, Enterprise, Edu, Business, and Pro workspaces, but you can also use ChatGPT’s prompt box dictation feature to ask it to transcribe voice messages or turn them into bullet points.

items.text:
Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd
- Published
"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."
Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.
The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.
He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.
The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.
Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.
So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?
There is a clear non-negotiable.
"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.
- Manchester won't always be blue - Pochettino 
  - Published1 day ago
'Making the players feel like winners again'
It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.
Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.
United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.
One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.
"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.
"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.
"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."
Fixing a leaky defence
That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.
Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?
The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.
Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.
Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.
Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.
Then there is Dalot.
The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.
It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.
However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.
Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.
Solving the Fernandes issue
Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.
The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.
He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.
For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.
What else? Can any youngsters step up?
Fernandes' status affects other areas. Carrick never seemed convinced by Andrey Santos, a £50m summer arrival from Chelsea. But with £70m Carlos Baleba out for an extended period, a partner needs to be found in midfield for Kobbie Mainoo.
Tielemans did not seem to have the running ability for the role, and Amorim wouldn't pick Mainoo with Fernandes.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO puts AI’s circular financing boom to the test
items.summary:
Arriving at public markets today, Anthropic’s IPO is poised to raise billions for the company and its investors. But the biggest surprise may be just how much of that money will end up going to supplier-investors.
Amazon and Google, two of Anthropic’s largest infrastructure partners, hold stakes val
items.text:
Arriving at public markets today, Anthropic’s IPO is poised to raise billions for the company and its investors. But the biggest surprise may be just how much of that money will end up going to supplier-investors.
Amazon and Google, two of Anthropic’s largest infrastructure partners, hold stakes valued around a combined $307.9 billion at the company’s updated IPO price of $83 per share. Amazon, which invested $18 billion into the AI startup, would see its 14.7% stake hit upwards of $159 billion, while Google’s 13.7% stake is valued at nearly $149 billion, according to share ownership figures disclosed in Anthropic’s IPO prospectus.
A handful of other AI infrastructure providers are also positioned to benefit. Nvidia, AMD, Microsoft, Broadcom, Micron, and TSMC have joined Google in committing $26 billion to Anthropic at its IPO price in a private placement.
In total, Google has invested $12.3 billion into Anthropic since 2023, with another promised $30 billion dependent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. And with the exception of TSMC, Anthropic has announced multi-billion-dollar strategic partnerships with its other infrastructure supplier investors — including Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Microsoft, and Micron — that would see Anthropic purchasing their products.
This is the circular financing that has made some observers so skeptical of the AI boom. These companies are not just investors; they’re also Anthropic’s biggest suppliers. It might look like Amazon and Google are putting billions into Anthropic, but they get that money right back when Anthropic needs to train a model or serve Claude to users. From afar, it looks like unprecedented revenue growth for cloud companies and unprecedented fundraising from Anthropic — but it’s just the same money passing from one pocket to another.
Today’s IPO marks a critical change in that financing system, the moment it might just become self-sustaining. Those investments appear to have paid off, and are now liquid. Anthropic is still operating at a net loss of tens of billions of dollars each quarter — but it will no longer be suppliers and private investors footing the bill. Now, capital will come from a mix of public-market investors and corporate bonds, neither of which have the conflicts-of-interest that caused concerns before.
And critically, the company’s new bottom line looks pretty good.
Once it debuts, Anthropic is expected to have about $220 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, including proceeds from its IPO and the $26 billion private placement. Anthropic also has the ability to pay for future commitments in stock.
Joey Brookhart, who leads the Tokenomics team at SemiAnalysis, estimates that Anthropic needs roughly $280 billion in cumulative revenue over the next four years to pay for its compute bill, which Brookhart said is “achievable given where they will be next year from a revenue perspective.”
“The ownership stake is very worthwhile, and those companies no longer need any more support from [suppliers],” Brookhart told TechCrunch. “Amazon doesn’t need to prop them up anymore. The revenue is all coming from other customers.”
That doesn’t mean the server bills are going down, though. Anthropic has already committed to spend $900 billion, primarily for compute and infrastructure, according to a regulatory filing. Certain agreements have termination provisions, but Brookhart thinks the company is in a strong position to pay up.
On the other side, Anthropic generated $17 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue, putting the company on pace for a $68 billion annualized rate for the year. If Anthropic continues to grow at its current trajectory, Brookhart believes it could easily cover the gap needed to fund its compute.
Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, agreed.
“By the time the IPO is done, Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had,” Luria told TechCrunch, noting that the firm raised around $141 billion in capital and will take home around $91.7 billion in net proceeds at $83 per share. “And they’re not burning cash. They’re just going to have a war chest.”
A public listing will make Anthropic a more credible borrower, making it easier to raise money outside of public markets, says Brookhart. That’s despite recent reports that creditors might not see Anthropic as “investment-grade” material.
Luria distinguished between Anthropic’s supplier investments and neoclouds like CoreWeave, which he sees as more purely supported by circular financing. “CoreWeave wouldn’t exist if Nvidia didn’t prop them up, and it probably won’t exist if Nvidia doesn’t bail them out,” Luria said.
Brookhart also pushed back on describing Anthropic’s financing as purely circular, saying it was still “additive to the ecosystem.”
For both analysts, the biggest risk to Anthropic is simply that it will lose the AI race. Right now, the company’s growth is fueled by its status at the frontier of generative AI — but if it’s overtaken by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, or even cheap open-weight models, that could change fast. As Luria put it: “If we’re all using other people’s models, then Anthropic’s not worth a trillion and a half dollars. It’s worth nothing.”
But regardless of who wins the frontier, compute suppliers will likely be just fine. Neither Brookhart nor Luria believe Anthropic’s growth is at risk, despite some arguments that cheaper tokens and more competition will directly affect the AI company’s bottom line.
“For Amazon and Google, the risk isn’t actually that high because in that scenario, we’re using other models,” Luria said. “I’m arguing we’re going to use a lot more AI. I don’t know if it’s all Anthropic’s AI….That’s still going to come from a data center managed by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.”

items.title: Will Pochettino fix Manchester United? Will Unwin is answering your questions – live
items.summary:
Will is here!
Will Unwin is online now answering all your Manchester United questions. It’s not too late to get involved, ask yours here.
As Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge at Anfield, the Guardian’s Will Unwin is taking your questions on Manchester United’s new head coach,
items.text:
Will is here!
Will Unwin is online now answering all your Manchester United questions. It’s not too late to get involved, ask yours here.
As Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge at Anfield, the Guardian’s Will Unwin is taking your questions on Manchester United’s new head coach, the crisis he inherits and what comes next.
Ask a question: log in or sign up here
salfordexile66 asks: United follower since 1974. For the first time that I can remember I have no sense of optimism at the arrival of the new manager. Don’t get me wrong, I think he is a capable guy, but the manager isn’t the problem. It never has been since 2005. I feel that the only way to get the owners to quit is a full-on boycott of games by season ticket holders, ie leave just after the game starts and don’t return, coupled with ceasing to buy merchandise for the foreseeable future. What do you think?
Will: Fans are very loyal, and the badge of honour that comes with attending every game is a difficult one to shake, especially when clubs threaten to take away season tickets from those who don’t attend enough matches. United, and other clubs, know that.
United are bigger than a football club and have a plethora of revenue streams. They have been an underwhelming team in a big stadium for a long time, and their global fanbase has not been affected. But I do think one thing that would damage the product is swathes of empty seats at Old Trafford. It is a sports entertainment business at the Theatre of Dreams, and if the seats are empty, it becomes more depressing and harder to buy into. So a mass boycott would have a huge impact on the club.
Fan power has been decreasing with each passing year, which means bolder plans of action are needed. United supporters have done a fine job with their marches and banners, so it does feel as though they will eventually take further steps.
MademoiselleK asks: Do you think Pochettino will see Rashford as a key player in his plans, or want to bring in a replacement?
Will: Pochettino will certainly give Rashford every chance to prove himself. For the players it is a chance to start again but Rashford needs to show he can maintain professionalism and produce on the pitch. He is a quality player, who has the capabilities of being a gamechanger at the top level.
Pochettino will not write anyone off without giving him a go. Rashford had a decent season at Barcelona and has offered a glimpse or two since returning but without any notable output in terms of goals and assists. His contract is long and expensive, making him difficult to sell, so the player and club need it to work.
dNazareth asks: I remember reading that one of Sir Alex Ferguson’s greatest achievements was transitioning into more of a director-level role, allowing his assistants to implement their own ideas about how the team should play and modernise the tactics without losing the club’s identity. Is the director of football role the weakest link in Manchester United’s current hierarchy?
kiya asks along similar lines: Given how often Poch referred to himself as United’s “head coach” (a point of friction at Spurs), how often do you request interviews with the real power at the club – Wilcox, Berrada or Ratcliffe? What do you think of Wilcox and Berrada? Is it true they were appointed mainly on their success at Man City?
Will: I have written about the role of Jason Wilcox few times before. Martínez thrust him into the limelight in recent weeks, and he has faced the ire of fans, whose chants about the director of football have featured some choice language. The results on the pitch show there is a problem, but the blame has fallen on successive head coaches despite clear failings in how the squad has been recruited.
Wilcox desperately needs Pochettino to be the catalyst for success. Otherwise he will face a lot more questions, and may find his position untenable sooner rather than later. He had little experience of a senior first-team role before joining United, and little he has done since suggests he is capable of being a leadership figure at a Champions League club.
When it comes to signings, few come from outside the Premier League, which means United are always going to have to overpay. Brighton, who are second, have been built on clever scouting and data analysis, while United look at who did well at Brentford or Wolves the previous season. United need to change something about their recruitment, and someone like George Syrianos at Nottingham Forest, who thinks outside the box, would be worth considering.
Requests have been made to speak to Wilcox, but it feels like a futile gesture. As for the City connection, I think United saw the success there and wanted some of that influence.
Whosdatdandare asks: With Poch becoming the new fall guy who will get a tune out of the team before asking to be backed in the transfer market, being told we can’t afford player X and then leaving, how does the club remove the true issue? … So, how do you solve a problem like the Glazers and Ineos? No change of manager will do it.
Will: The fans point of view will be to remove the ownership, as they have made the case for. They are seen as a problem for numerous reasons, from taking money out of the club to moving fans out of their seats to make way for more lucrative hospitality clients. Nothing will really change at United until the team becomes the full focus and the right football brains are in the most significant jobs. With the current setup, the only way of things getting better is if there is constant success but the club is not built on such foundations.
Books have been written on the subject of United since the Glazers came to Old Trafford, so will offer some further reading:
We’ve had many questions about United’s finances. kapsiolaaaaa asks: Is there still the spending power to support Poch? Can United go out and buy a £70m player in January without selling someone? What about wages?
Dmitriverlouanne asks along similar line

items.text:
Man Utd latest financial results revealed as revenue and wages increase
Manchester United's latest financial results for the first fiscal quarter of 2027 covered three months up to September 30; it included the summer transfer window and their return to the Champions League, but not the sacking of Michael Carrick and arrival of Mauricio Pochettino
Thursday 19 November 2026 14:46, UK
Manchester United have released their latest financial results, with revenue and wages increasing.
The first quarter fiscal 2027 report covered three months up to September 30. It included the summer transfer window but not the sacking of Michael Carrick and subsequent hiring of Mauricio Pochettino.
It does include the club's return to the Champions League. However, only one of these matches were at home - a 4-0 win against Sabah. They played four further games at Old Trafford, and three away.

- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱

Manchester United's total revenues rose 4.1 per cent to £146.1m compared to the same period last year, while wages are up 8.6 per cent to £79.9m.
The club's loss after tax increased by 174.2 per cent to £18.1m, with interest paid down 32 per cent to £14.5m.
Non-current borrowings - the debts associated when the Glazer family bought the club 21 years ago - are up 19.2 per cent from $650m (£481.2m) to $775m (£577.4m), primarily as a result of refinancing. Current borrowings are down from £268m to £207.1m.
In terms of personnel, player sale profits down went down 54 per cent to £20.7m. The net expenditure on intangible assets - namely players - increased by £43.3m to £143.1m.
There was 17.7 per cent in broadcasting revenue - up from £29.9m to £35.2m - which likely coincides with Manchester United's return to the Champions League.
Matchday revenue is also up 2.3 per cent from £26.2m to £26.8m, although sponsorship revenue went down three per cent from £47m to £45.6m after the men's team had a smaller pre-season tour. Retail and merchandising also went up 3.5 per cent from £37.2m to £38.5m.
Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada said of the results: "Our revenue remains strong and on track, while we continue to grow sustainably.
"We are pleased to welcome Mauricio Pochettino and his staff to the club and our priority is to support them as we look continuously to improve our performances on the pitch.
"We are pleased with the progress Eva Olid has made with our women's team and how well the team has adapted to her approach."

items.summary:
Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.
With the biggest IPO of all time, An
items.text:
Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone.
With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
Anthropic’s unusual power structure gives it free rein to shape AI’s future.
With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
Anthropic’s unusual power structure gives it free rein to shape AI’s future.
Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power.
One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight.
Anthropic has spent years billing itself as different from, and more careful than, other AI companies. In theory, this extends to its plan for going public. It’s registered as a Public Benefit Corporation, which means Anthropic’s board has a responsibility to balance its mission against shareholder wealth maximization. As my colleague Robert Hart has discussed before, it has also developed a highly unusual power structure.
Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), introduced in 2023, and its founders have controlling voting rights, meaning they’d never be able to be voted out by shareholders even as a public company. A special class of stock, Class T, allows a small group of trustees — the members of the LTBT — the “authority to select and remove a portion of” Anthropic’s board. They exist outside typical shareholder pressure and theoretically are a check for the founders, tasked with a mission to “balance the financial interests of our stockholders and our public benefit purpose at key junctures where we expect the consequences of our decisions to reach far beyond Anthropic.”
The reality is significantly more complicated. The LTBT technically chooses four members of Anthropic’s seven-person board, for instance, but one of those four effectively needs to be approved by Anthropic’s founders, leaving the trust short of straightforward majority control. There are also stipulations about nominating or removing a director: the LTBT must provide its decision with 30 days’ notice to the company’s “nominating and corporate governance committee,” which consists of three members: co-founder Daniela Amodei (who is chair of the committee), Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, and Anthropic investor Yasmin Razavi.
Though the LTBT members are “financially disinterested” in the company, there’s also nothing stopping Anthropic from hypothetically hiring away a trustee and paying them a lot of money to work for the company. Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar (a former trustee) joined Anthropic in August as its Chief Global Affairs Officer, and OpenAI has in the past hired a former board member, Fidji Simo, to an executive position within the company. One could imagine a scenario in which, if a trustee was “looking a little bit too activist-y or something, they could just make that trustee an offer with millions of dollars in effective compensation that would entail stepping down from the trust, and that’s one way that they could have some oversight over this,” said Tyler Johnston, founder of The Midas Project, a nonprofit AI industry watchdog.
Although the LTBT is billed as a way to check Anthropic’s leadership, to some outside observers, the fine print looks shaky. “The trust, since it doesn’t have a financial interest in Anthropic, could theoretically use its power with three slash four directors to keep the company on mission,” says Ann Lipton, law professor at the University of Colorado Law School and an expert in corporate governance. “One might question how likely that is to occur.”
Moreover, Lipton questions whether the trust would know enough to gauge when to hit the brakes on a company plan or product even if they did have such authority. The four listed LTBT members aren’t known to be AI experts: they include former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke, foreign policy analyst Richard Fontaine, experimental physicist Christopher Stubbs, and former GiveWell executive Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT. “I’m not convinced that the trustees or the directors that they appoint have the insight into AI and AI development to be able to make these choices,” Lipton says. “They’re very prestigious people, but what does Ben Bernanke know about AI?”
Several experts compared Anthropic’s LTBT to OpenAI’s nonprofit board before Altman’s ouster: “The powers, or lack thereof, of the Long-Term Benefit Trust … [are] analogous in some ways to the powers that the OpenAI nonprofit has,” said The Midas Project’s Johnston. Of course, that board’s decision to oust OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ended up leading, days later, to Altman’s return as CEO and the majority of the board’s resignation and replacement.
But there’s a notable difference between that and the LTBT. Before OpenAI’s restructuring, its nonprofit board had the ability to step in and guide day-to-day decisions at the company when deemed nece

items.text:
Nations Championship: Will Joseph retains England place vs New Zealand's All Blacks as Henry Pollock dropped amid nine changes
Steve Borthwick makes nine changes to England XV for visit of All Blacks in Nations Championship on Saturday (2.10pm); Fin Smith, George Furbank, Tommy Freeman, Seb Atkinson, Jamie George, Fin Baxter, Joe Heyes, Ollie Chessum, Ben Curry all return; Will Joseph keeps place on wing
Thursday 19 November 2026 14:00, UK
Will Joseph has retained his place on the wing for England's Nations Championship Test against New Zealand on Saturday, with Fin Smith among those restored and Henry Pollock dropped to the bench.
Joseph, who missed out on a place in England's matchday 23 for their 45-22 defeat of Australia a fortnight ago, started in last week's crushing 78-15 success over Japan, scoring five tries.
The 24-year-old picked up just his second Test cap in that victory at Twickenham, and his first since July 2022 under Eddie Jones. He moves from right to left wing for the visit of the All Blacks.
Elsewhere fly-half Smith, full-back George Furbank, wing Tommy Freeman, centre Seb Atkinson, hooker Jamie George, props Fin Baxter and Joe Heyes and back-rowers Ollie Chessum and Ben Curry all return as part of nine changes by Steve Borthwick.
Pollock, who made just his second Test start for England in 15 caps last week, drops down to the replacements bench.
Outside-centre Henry Slade, scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet, lock and captain Maro Itoje, second-row Alex Coles - who shifts back alongside Itoje from blindside flanker - and No 8 Ben Earl keep their places.
Alongside Pollock, the replacements bench is made up of hooker Luke Cowan-Dickie, loosehead Ellis Genge, tighthead Will Stuart, lock George Martin, back-row Greg Fisilau, scrum-half Ben Spencer and fly-half/full-back Marcus Smith.
"There are few bigger occasions in international rugby than facing New Zealand," said Borthwick.
"It's a fixture that always carries a special significance, and one that the players are hugely looking forward to.
"We know the quality New Zealand have in their team. We've prepared for the very best version of them, knowing the challenge they will bring and the level we'll need to reach to get the result we want."
England squad to face New Zealand in Nations Championship
England: 15 George Furbank, 14 Tommy Freeman, 13 Henry Slade, 12 Seb Atkinson, 11 Will Joseph, 10 Fin Smith, 9 Jack van Poortvliet; 1 Fin Baxter, 2 Jamie George, 3 Joe Heyes, 4 Maro Itoje, 5 Alex Coles, 6 Ollie Chessum, 7 Ben Curry, 8 Ben Earl.
Replacements: 16 Luke Cowan-Dickie, 17 Ellis Genge, 18 Will Stuart, 19 George Martin, 20 Greg Fisilau, 21 Henry Pollock, 22 Ben Spencer, 23 Marcus Smith.
All Blacks make eight changes for England clash
For the All Blacks, they have brought Codie Taylor back as captain and veteran Beauden Barrett is set to win his 150th cap as coach Dave Rennie makes eight changes.
Rennie has considerably strengthened the side after their upset loss to Wales last weekend, which left them one point ahead of South Africa in the Southern Hemisphere standings.
Taylor, who takes over from Barrett as skipper, is one of two changes in the front row for Saturday's clash. He replaces Asafo Aumua at hooker, and prop Ethan de Groot regains his berth at loosehead in place of George Bower.
Fabian Holland takes over from Josh Lord among the locks, while Tupou Vaa'i comes back for Anton Segner in the back row.
Damian McKenzie returns at fly-half and Cam Roigard at scrum-half, with last week's half-back pairing of Richie Mo'unga and Cortez Ratima dropping to the bench.
Jordie Barrett and Will Jordan return from injury among the backs, while centre Anton Lienert-Brown will earn his 100th cap.

items.title: Superhuman pushes its Go assistant everywhere
items.summary: Productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products. Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) is going in the same direction with the rollout of features, including a personalized Go assi
items.text:
Productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products. Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) is going in the same direction with the rollout of features, including a personalized Go assistant, making agents available in Docs, and third-party agent integrations.
While some of the company’s AI features have faced criticism, Superhuman started pushing its Go assistant after its rebranding last year. With the new rollout, it is making Go learn context across different apps and give better personalized suggestions for prompts. Superhuman is revamping its onboarding flow to let users connect their preferred tools and load context about their work upfront.
The assistant works inline with the cursor — just like Grammarly does — and also manages other agents. Superhuman is also making the agent proactive, which means it looks for your schedule, keeps an eye on your email, and even drafts responses. The updated Go agent also learns users’ writing styles and responds accordingly in email and Docs.
The productivity company is adding 20 new connected agents, including DeepL, Legora, Amplitude, Databricks, and Blackboard, through its Go SDK.
The company is also thinking about adding AI to different products, including Docs and Superhuman Mail. In Docs, all Go agents work natively, and you can set them off to work on different tasks in the background. Users can also set routines to trigger workflows based on events.
Until now, Mail has used AI as its central tool, which is being replaced by Go. Users can also do enterprise search by using data from the company knowledge base and connected tools. Go also uses this context to form drafts and organize the inbox across Google and Outlook accounts.
Superhuman acquired notetaker Fathom in September to add more context to its suite. The company is now rolling out live collaborative notetaking, which would be shared across the team. Plus, Go can now make decisions post-meeting, like forming an initial draft of a proposal.
The company’s CEO, Shishir Mehrotra, said that Go has had good momentum with over 1 million active users. There are a host of agents now that are vying for users’ attention on both the personal and professional front. Mehrotra thinks that while Go is more work-focused, it can help with personal emails and schedules.
“One of the reasons why these assistants have been popular is that they treat you as a whole person and recognize that we need to cover both extremes. Go is definitely more work-focused than some of the tools coming out of the pure consumer ecosystem. It doesn’t mean we draw the boundary at helping you with your personal tasks or helping you with your calendar or all of your email,” he told TechCrunch over a call.
While Go might not directly compete with the likes of Instinct, Muse, and Fo, Superhuman wants users to choose its assistant over something like OpenAI’s Dots or Claude Duet.
